cards.name: Andromeda
cards.summary: Andromeda is a large northern constellation representing the daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia, who was chained to a rock to be eaten by a sea monster. It is one of the forty-eight figures catalogued by Ptolemy and is most prominent during autumn evenings.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find this figure between latitudes ninety and minus thirty-eight, reaching its highest point around November. Look for the stars Alpheratz, Mirach, and Almach, which form a pattern that some see as an immense Dipper or a Cross. It is bordered by Cassiopeia and Perseus to the north, Pegasus and Lacerta to the west, and Pisces and Triangulum to the south.
cards.mythology: In Greek myth, Andromeda was chained to a rock as punishment for her mother's boast that her own beauty was superior to the Nereids. The original figure was described as a young woman bound to the rocks at Joppa, where ancient authors claimed the marks of her chains could still be seen. While the legend is often associated with Greece, its origins may date back more than two millenniums before our era to the Babylonian story of Bel Marduk and the dragon Tiamat.

quotes.text: For there, too, wheels that woeful form of Andromeda, enstarred beneath her mother. Thou hast not to wait for a night, I ween, whereon to see her more distinct! So bright is her head and so clearly marked are both the shoulders, the tips of her feet and all her belt.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Andromeda, the Woman Chained, The Ἀνδρομέδη of Aratos and Ἀνδρομέδα of Eratosthenes, Hipparchos, and Ptolemy, represents in the sky the daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia, king and queen of Aethiopia, chained in exposure to the sea monster as punishment of her mother's boast of beauty superior to that of the Nereids.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Andromeda

quotes.text: Uplifted and outspread there for all time are those hands of hers.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Antlia
cards.summary: Antlia is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere that represents an air pump. Its name means pump in Latin and Greek and was originally established as Antlia Pneumatica by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find this inconspicuous constellation south of Hydra and Crater, bordering the sails of the ship Argo Navis. It is highest in the sky at 9pm during April and is fully visible to anyone located between latitudes 50 degrees north and 90 degrees south.
cards.mythology: There is no traditional myth associated with this figure. It was introduced in the 18th century by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille as Machine Pneumatique, later Latinized to Machina Pneumatica or Antlia Pneumatica.

quotes.text: Antlia Pneumatica, the Air Pump, is La Caille's Machine Pneumatique, at first Latinized as Machina Pneumatica (which occurs in Burritt, and is the Italian name); but astronomers know it as simple Antlia. In Germany it is the Luft Pumpe.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Antlia Pneumatica

cards.name: Apus
cards.summary: Apus is a small constellation in the southern sky that represents a bird-of-paradise. Its name means "without feet" in Greek because the bird-of-paradise was once wrongly believed to lack feet. It was first depicted on a celestial globe by Petrus Plancius in 1598 and later charted by Johann Bayer in 1603.
cards.howToFind: Apus lies immediately below the Southern Triangle, about thirteen degrees from the South pole. It is bordered by Triangulum Australe, Pavo, and Octans, among other southern figures. The constellation is fully visible between latitudes of minus ninety and eight degrees and is highest at nine PM around July. Observers can look for the star named Paradys within its figure.
cards.mythology: There is no classical Greek myth for this constellation as it was introduced in the late 16th century by Petrus Plancius. The figure represents a bird-of-paradise, which was once fabled to be legless. In China, it was known as the Curious Sparrow and the Little Wonder Bird.

quotes.text: Apus, the Bird of Paradise, or Apous, as Caesius wrote it from the Greek, lies immediately below the Southern Triangle, about 13° from the South pole. It is the French Oiseau de Paradis; the German Paradies Vogel; and the Italian Uccello Paradiso.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Apus

quotes.text: Its avian original is found only in the Papuan Islands, and the title is from Ἄπους, Without Feet, for the ancient Greek swallow, but well applied to this bird that has been thus fabled, as witness Keats' "legless birds of paradise,"
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Apus

cards.name: Aquarius
cards.summary: Aquarius is an equatorial constellation of the zodiac, between Capricornus and Pisces. Its name is Latin for "water-carrier" or "cup-carrier", and it is one of the oldest of the recognized constellations along the zodiac. It was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy.
cards.howToFind: Aquarius is highest at 9pm around October and is fully visible between latitudes 64 and -87. The figure is marked by the stars Sadalsuud, Sadalmelik, Skat, and Safina, with the right hand of the figure stretched by the head of Pegasus. A familiar Y-shaped pattern known as the Urn is formed by the stars Sadachbia, Zeta, Eta, and Pi Aquarii.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, this constellation has been identified as Deucalion of the Greek Deluge or as Ganymedes, the beautiful Phrygian boy who was the cup-bearer of Jove. Pindar asserted that it symbolized the genius of the fountains of the Nile. In Babylonia, it was associated with the eleventh month and the Curse of Rain, while in China it was later known as the Dark Warrior and Hero.

quotes.text: The constellation immemorially has been represented, even on very early Babylonian stones, as a man, or boy, pouring water from a bucket or urn, with an appropriate towel in the left hand, the human figure sometimes being omitted;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Aquarius

quotes.text: Like a slight flow of water here and there Scattered around, bright stars revolve but small;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Aquarius

quotes.text: Round the prancing Horse range the two Fishes. By the Horse’s head is stretched the right hand of Hydrochoüs. He is behind Aegoceros, who is set in front and further down, where the mighty Sun turns.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Aquila
cards.summary: Aquila is a constellation on the celestial equator that represents an eagle. It is an ancient figure supposed to be represented on a Euphratean stone from 1200 B.C. and is known in Latin as the Armor-bearing Bird of Jove.
cards.howToFind: Aquila is highest at 9pm during August and is fully visible between latitudes -72 and 78. An observer can identify it by the bright star Altair, which is flanked by Alshain and Tarazed to form a five-degree line known as the Family of Aquila. The figure is shown flying toward the east across the Milky Way, situated westward from Delphinus and near the constellations of Sagittarius and Sagitta.
cards.mythology: In Greco-Roman mythology, this figure represents the bird that carried the thunderbolts of Zeus or the one ordered to attack Prometheus. Some stories identify the eagle as the agent that carried Ganymede to the heavens to serve the gods. Other traditions associate the stars with the Draught Oxen of Chinese lore or a Korean prince separated from his bride by the River of the Sky.

quotes.text: Jove for the prince of birds decreed, And carrier of his thunder, too, The bird whom golden Ganymede Too well for trusty agent knew.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Aquila

quotes.text: In it are the Belt of the well-starred Orion and the coil of the gleaming Hydra: in it, too, the dim-lit Crater and the Crow and the scanty-starred Claws and the knees of Ophiuchus are borne.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: But it has no share in the Eagle, but near it flies the mighty messenger of Zeus. Facing the Eagle wheel the head and neck of the Horse.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Ara
cards.summary: Ara is a southern constellation representing an altar, known to the Greeks as Bomos. It was one of the forty-eight classical constellations described by Ptolemy and is now recognized as one of the eighty-eight modern constellations.
cards.howToFind: Located south of the glowing sting of Scorpius, the figure is situated between Telescopium and Norma. It is best observed in July from latitudes south of twenty-two degrees north, appearing briefly above the southern horizon. The stars Beta, Gamma, Delta, Epsilon, and Zeta are said to mark the flame of the altar rising toward the south.
cards.mythology: In Greek mythology, the gods created this altar in heaven to swear mutual vows during their war against the Titans. It has also been identified as the altar of Dionysus, the altar of Noah, or one of the altars raised by Moses. Some traditions represent it as a censer or a brazier, while others suggest it served as a celestial lighthouse similar to the Alexandrian Pharos.

quotes.text: Below the fiery sting of the dread monster, Scorpion, and near the South is hung the Altar. Brief is the space thou wilt behold it above the horizon: for it rises over against Arcturus.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Rais'd this Altar, and the Form appears With Incense loaded, and adorn'd with Stars;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Ara

quotes.text: But the Altar even beyond aught else hath ancient Night, weeping the woe of men, set to be a mighty sing of storm at sea.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Aries
cards.summary: Aries is a mid-sized zodiacal constellation of the northern celestial hemisphere representing a ram. One of the forty-eight figures described by Ptolemy in the second century, it is known in Latin as Aries and in Greek as Krios.
cards.howToFind: Aries is located between Pisces to the west and Taurus to the east, sitting southward a little from the triangle of Triangulum. An observer can trace the figure by the belt of Andromeda, as the ram is set a little below her. Look for the noticeable triangle formed by the stars Hamal, Sheratan, and Bharani, which culminates in December and is fully visible between latitudes ninety degrees and minus fifty-nine degrees.
cards.mythology: In classical lore, this ram bore the hero Phrixus and his sister Helle away from the wrath of their stepmother Ino. During the flight, Helle fell into the sea, which was thereafter named the Hellespont in her memory. Upon reaching Colchis, Phrixus sacrificed the ram and hung its fleece in the Grove of Ares, where it turned to gold and became the object of the Argonauts' quest. Other traditions associate the figure with the Egyptian god Amon or the ram caught in a thicket from the story of Abraham.

quotes.text:
First Golden Aries shines (who whilst he swam
Lost part of's Freight, and gave the Sea a Name);
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Aries

quotes.text:
The Ram having pass'd the Sea serenely shines,
And leads the Year, the Prince of all the Signs.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Aries

quotes.text: There too are the most swift courses of the Ram, who, pursued through the longest circuit, runs not a whit slower than the Bear Cynosura – himself weak and starless as on a moonlit night
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Auriga
cards.summary: Auriga is a large northern constellation representing the Charioteer or Wagoner. It was one of the original forty-eight figures listed by Ptolemy and is often depicted as a man holding a whip, though he is frequently shown without an actual chariot.
cards.howToFind: Look for a prominent figure leaning forward at the left hand of the Twins, situated between Perseus and Gemini. Its brightest star, Capella, is the most northern of all first-magnitude stars and is accompanied by a small triangle of stars known as the Kids. The figure is further defined by the stars Menkalinan, Mahasim, Hassaleh, and Saclateni, while Elnath marks the Charioteer's foot and the tip of the Bull's horn.
cards.mythology: The constellation is frequently identified as Erichthonius, the fourth king of Athens and son of Vulcan, who invented the four-horse chariot to overcome his lameness. Other traditions associate the figure with Myrtilus, the charioteer of Oenomaus, or Hippolytus. The figure also carries the holy Goat on his left shoulder, which legend tells gave the breast to Zeus, and the Kids upon his wrist.

quotes.text: Near the bent Bull a Seat the Driver claims, Whose skill conferr'd his Honour and his Names. His Art great jove admir'd, when first he drove His rattling Carr, and fix't the Youth above.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Auriga

quotes.text: But if it be thy wish to mark Charioteer and his stars, and if the fame has come to thee of the Goat herself and the Kids, who often on the darkening deep have seen men storm-tossed, thou wilt find him in all his might, leaning forward at the left hand of the Twins.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: But not yet depart the Kids of the Charioteer and the Arm-borne (Olenian) Goat; by his great hand they shine, and are eminent beyond all his other limbs in raising storms, when they fare with the sun.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Boötes
cards.summary: Boötes is a large northern constellation representing a herdsman or plowman, a figure that has been recognized for nearly three thousand years. Its name is derived from the Greek words for ox and to drive, or from a term meaning clamorous, referring to the shouts of a driver to his oxen.
cards.howToFind: Look for this figure in the northern sky during June, when it is highest in the evening. Its primary star, Arcturus, is located beneath the belt of the figure and is bright beyond the others. The constellation is bordered by Ursa Major and Virgo, and its stars Nekkar and Seginus mark the head and shoulder respectively.
cards.mythology: The figure is often identified as Arcas, the son of the nymph Kallisto, or as the Athenian Icarius who was placed in the sky by Bacchus. Some traditions associate him with Philomelus, the son of Ceres, or the giant hunter Nimrod. Because he appears to drive the Great Bear around the pole, he is frequently called the Bear-guard or the Keeper of the Wain. Would you like a summary of the next constellation?

quotes.text: Behind Helice, like to one that drives, is borne along Arctophylax whom men also call Boötes, since he seems to lay hand on the wain-like Bear. Very bright is he all; but beneath his belt wheels a star, bright beyond the others, Arcturus himself.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Arctophylax, on earth Boötes named, Sheds o'er the Arctic car his silver light.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Bootes

quotes.text: Slow Boötes drives his ling'ring Teams;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Bootes

cards.name: Caelum
cards.summary: Caelum is a faint constellation in the southern sky that represents a chisel or graving tool. It was introduced in the 1750s by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille and is the eighth-smallest constellation.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Caelum between the constellations of Columba and Eridanus, directly south of the stars that once formed Sceptrum Brandenburgicum. It is highest in the evening sky around January and is fully visible to anyone located between 41 degrees north and 90 degrees south latitude. The figure is composed of faint stars and is bordered by Lepus, Pictor, Dorado, and Horologium.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient mythology associated with this constellation. It was formed by La Caille in the 18th century from stars in the southern hemisphere. While originally known as Caelum Sculptorium, the name was briefly changed by Burritt to Praxiteles in early editions of his book.

quotes.text: Caelum or Scalptorium, the Burin or Graving-Tool, sometimes incorrectly written Cela sculptoria, is the French Burin, the Italian Bulino, and the German Grabstichel.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Caelum

quotes.text: Its name means "chisel" in Latin, and it was formerly known as Caelum Sculptorium ; it is a rare word, unrelated to the far more common Latin caelum, meaning "sky", "heaven", or "atmosphere".

cards.name: Camelopardalis
cards.summary: Camelopardalis is a large but faint constellation of the Northern Sky representing a giraffe. It was introduced in 1612 or 1613 by Petrus Plancius and is described as being long, faint, and straggling like its namesake. The name recognized by the International Astronomical Union matches the genitive form of the word.
cards.howToFind: This constellation is best seen in January and is fully visible between latitudes 90 and -4. It stretches from the pole-star to Perseus, Auriga, and the Lynx, with its hind quarters located within the Milky Way. Observers can look for the star Shaowei or find the lucida located 20 degrees north of Capella, below the left hock of the animal.
cards.mythology: There is no classical Greek myth for this constellation as it was a modern creation. Bartschius, who published the figure in 1614, wrote that it represented the Camel that brought Rebecca to Isaac. In Chinese astronomy, the area contained seven asterisms including the State Umbrella, the Four Official Supporters of the Throne, and Unostentatious Virtue.

quotes.text: Camelopardalis or Camelopardus, the Giraffe, the French Girafe and Italian Giraffa, is long, faint, and straggling like its namesake. It stretches from the pole-star to Perseus, Auriga, and the Lynx, the hind quarters within the Milky Way.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Camelopardalis

quotes.text: It was formed by Bartschius, who published it, in outline only, in 1614, and wrote that it represented to him the Camel that brought Rebecca to Isaac.

cards.name: Cancer
cards.summary: Cancer is a zodiacal constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere that represents a crab. It is the most inconspicuous figure in the zodiac and was once known as the Dark Sign, quaintly described as black and without eyes.
cards.howToFind: Cancer lies between Gemini to the west and Leo to the east, also bordering Lynx, Hydra, and Canis Minor. It is highest at 9pm around March and is visible between latitudes 90 and -56. The figure is marked by stars including Tarf, Acubens, and the Aselli, which flank the faint mist of the Praesepe cluster.
cards.mythology: Mythology explains the figure's presence by the story that when the Crab was crushed by Hercules, for pinching his toes during his contest with the Hydra in the marsh of Lerna, Juno exalted it to the sky. Another tale links the constellation to the two Asses that helped the gods in their conflict with the giants and were rewarded with a place in the sky on either side of the Manger.

quotes.text: It is the most inconspicuous figure in the zodiac, and mythology apologizes for its being there by the story that when the Crab was crushed by Hercules, for pinching his toes during his contest with the Hydra in the marsh of Lerna, Juno exalted it to the sky
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Cancer

quotes.text: Watch, too, the Manger. Like a faint mist in the North it plays the guide beneath Cancer. Around it are borne two faintly gleaming stars, not far apart nor very near but distant to the view a cubit’s length, one on the North, while the other looks towards the South.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text:
A murky Manger with both stars
Shining unaltered is a sign of rain.
If while the northern Ass is dimmed
By vaporous shroud, he of the south gleam radiant,
Expect a south wind: the vaporous shroud and radiance
Exchanging stars harbinger Boreas.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Cancer

cards.name: Canes Venatici
cards.summary: Canes Venatici is a small northern constellation representing the hunting dogs of Boötes the Herdsman. It was created by Johannes Hevelius in the 17th century and its name is Latin for "hunting dogs".
cards.howToFind: The constellation is located between Boötes, Coma Berenices, and Ursa Major. It is highest at 9pm around May and is fully visible between latitudes -37 and 90 degrees. Observers can identify it by its two brightest stars, Cor Caroli and Chara, which mark the southern dog of the pair.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient myth for this constellation as it was introduced by Hevelius in the 17th century. He depicted the figure as two greyhounds, Asterion and Chara, held on a leash by Boötes to pursue the Bear around the pole. One star, Cor Caroli, was named by Halley in 1725 to honor Charles II at the suggestion of a court physician who claimed it shone with special brilliancy upon the king's return to London.

quotes.text: The more northern one is Asterion, Starry, from the little stars marking the body; and the other, which contains the two brightest stars, is Chara, as Dear to the heart of her master.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Canes Venatici

quotes.text: the usual illustration is of two Greyhounds held by a leash in the hand of Boötes, ready for pursuit of the Bear around the pole; their inventor thus reviving the idea that Boötes was a hunter.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Canes Venatici

cards.name: Canis Major
cards.summary: Canis Major is a southern constellation representing the greater dog and was included in the second century by Ptolemy among his 48 original figures. It is commonly depicted as one of two hounds following Orion the hunter through the sky, with the Milky Way passing through its borders.
cards.howToFind: The constellation is highest in the evening sky around February and is fully visible for observers between latitudes 57 degrees north and 90 degrees south. It is easily identified by the star Sirius, which marks the nose of the dog and is the brightest star in the heavens. The figure stands on its hind legs to the southeast of Orion and is bordered by the constellations Columba, Lepus, Monoceros, and Puppis.
cards.mythology: In early classical lore, the figure represented Laelaps, the hound of Actaeon or the nymph Procris, famed for a speed that so gratified Jove he transferred the dog to the sky. It is also identified as the dog of Orion pursuing the Hare in an unending race. Other traditions associate the constellation with the dog of Tobias from the Book of Tobit or the royal Saint David.

quotes.text: The constant Scorcher comes as in pursuit, . . . and rises with it and its setting spies.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Canis Major

quotes.text: The tip of his terrible jaw is marked by a star that keenest of all blazes with a searing flame and him men call Seirius.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: One blazes through the brief bright summer's length, Lavishing life-heat from a flaming car.

cards.name: Canis Minor
cards.summary: Canis Minor is a small constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere that was included in the second century by Ptolemy. Its name is Latin for lesser dog, and the figure is commonly represented as following the hunter Orion. It was known to the Greeks as Procyon, as it rises before the companion dog star Sirius.
cards.howToFind: To locate this figure, look southeast from the feet of Gemini or beneath the Twins. The constellation is composed of a simple line between two stars, Procyon and Gomeisa, and is separated from Canis Major by Monoceros. It is fully visible between latitudes -76 and 90 degrees and is highest in the evening sky around February.
cards.mythology: In popular lore, this is Orion's second hound, though mythologists have also identified it as the dog of Actaeon or one of Diana's hounds. Another story identifies it as the dog Maera belonging to Icarius, or the favorite dog of Helen that was lost in the Euripus. An Arabic fable describes the figure as a sister of Sirius named Al Ghumaisa, the Dim, Watery-eyed, or Weeping One, who was left in tears after her sister crossed the Milky Way. In the 17th century, Julius Schiller imagined the constellation as the Paschal Lamb.

quotes.text: The Dog's-precursor, too, shines bright beneath the Twins.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Canis Minor

quotes.text: There, too, by the Hydra beneath the Twins brightly shines Procyon.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Who learned in matters astronomical, noteth not the great effects at the rising of the starre called the Litel Dogge.

cards.name: Capricornus
cards.summary: Capricornus is a zodiacal constellation whose name is Latin for horned goat. It is commonly represented as a sea goat, a mythical creature with the head and body of a goat and the tail of a fish. This figure is very ancient, appearing on Babylonian planispheres and gems as early as the 12th century B.C.
cards.howToFind: Capricornus is highest in the sky around September and is visible to observers between latitudes 62 and -90 degrees. It is located eastward from Sagittarius and is bordered by Aquila, Aquarius, Microscopium, and Piscis Austrinus. The constellation is noted for the duplicity of its brightest stars, Algedi and Dabih, which mark the head and horns, while Deneb Algedi and Nashira mark the tail.
cards.mythology: Eratosthenes identified the figure as the goat-footed Pan, who became half fish after plunging into the Nile to escape the monster Typhon. Platonists believed this constellation was the Gate of the Gods, through which the souls of men ascended to heaven after being released from their bodies. In other traditions, it was identified as the nurse of the youthful sun-god, a story that anticipated the myth of the infant Jupiter and Amalthea.

quotes.text: Then grievous blasts Break southward on the sea, when coincide The Goat and sun; and then a heaven-sent cold.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Capricornus

quotes.text: He is behind Aegoceros, who is set in front and further down, where the mighty Sun turns. In that month use not the open sea lest thou be engulfed in the waves.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Thy Cold (for thou o'er Winter Signs dost reign, Pull'st back the Sun, and send'st us Day again) Makes Brokers rich.

cards.name: Carina
cards.summary: Carina is a southern constellation whose name is Latin for the keel of a ship. It was originally the southern foundation of the much larger figure known as Argo Navis before that group was divided into three separate pieces. The other two divisions resulting from this split are Puppis and Vela.
cards.howToFind: Observers can locate this constellation in the southern sky, where it is highest at nine o'clock in the evening around March. It is fully visible to anyone between the latitudes of fifteen degrees north and ninety degrees south. The figure is marked by the bright stars Canopus, Miaplacidus, Avior, Naos, and Aspidiske, and it is bordered by neighbours such as Centaurus, Volans, and Puppis.
cards.mythology: Greek tradition identifies this figure as part of the ship built by Argos for Jason, the leader of the fifty Argonauts. Aided by Pallas Athene, the crew sailed from Thessaly to Colchis in search of the golden fleece, and the goddess eventually placed the vessel in the sky. Another account suggests it represents the first ship to sail the ocean, which carried Danaos and his fifty daughters from Egypt to Rhodes. Egyptian story instead claimed it was the ark that bore Isis and Osiris over the Deluge.

quotes.text: Sternforward thus is Jason's Argō drawn. This loss of its bow is said to have occurred when Argo pass'd Through Bosporus betwixt the justling rocks — the Symplegades, the Cyanean (azure), or the Planctae Rocks at the mouth of the Euxine Sea.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Argo Navis

quotes.text: Beside the tail of the Great Dog the ship Argo is hauled stern-foremost. For not hers is the proper course of a ship in motion, but she is borne backwards, reversed even as real ships, when already the sailors turn the stern to the land as they enter the haven, and every one back-paddles the ship, but she rushing sternward lays hold of the shore.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Argo Navis, the Ship Argo, generally plain Argo, — erroneously Argus, from confusion with its genitive case, — and Navis, is the German Schiff, the French Navire Argo, and the Italian Nave Argo.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Argo Navis

cards.name: Cassiopeia
cards.summary: Cassiopeia is a prominent northern constellation named after the vain queen of Greek mythology who was the mother of Andromeda. It is one of the original forty-eight constellations listed by Ptolemy and is easily recognizable by its five bright stars that form a distinctive W shape. The figure is also known as the Celestial M when it appears above the pole.
cards.howToFind: Observers can locate this constellation in the northern sky where it is highest at 9pm around November. It is fully visible between latitudes -13 and 90 degrees, situated near Cepheus, Andromeda, and Perseus. The primary figure is composed of the stars Schedar, Caph, Ruchbah, Segin, and Tiansi, which create a pattern resembling a folding door fitted with a key or a woman sitting in a chair.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, Cassiopeia was a queen who boasted of her unrivaled beauty, leading the sea-nymphs to seek a lesson in her humility. As punishment, she was placed in the sky bound to her seat so that she headlong plunges like a diver while going around the pole. This position ensures she sits head foremost like a tumbler to prevent her from falling out of her throne. During the seventeenth century, some religious scholars attempted to re-imagine the figure as Mary Magdalene or Deborah sitting under a palm tree.

quotes.text: The hapless Cassiepeia herself too hastes after the figure of her child. No longer in seemly wise does she shine upon her throne, feet and knees withal, but she headlong plunges like a diver, parted at the knees
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Hyginus, writing the word Cassiepia , described the figure as bound to her seat, and thus secured from falling out of it in going around the pole head downward
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Cassiopeia

quotes.text: E'en as a folding door, fitted within With key, is thrown back when the bolts are drawn.

cards.name: Centaurus
cards.summary: Centaurus is a bright and massive constellation in the southern sky representing a centaur, a creature that is half human and half horse. It was included among the forty-eight constellations listed by the second-century astronomer Ptolemy and remains one of the largest modern constellations.
cards.howToFind: Centaurus is fully visible between latitudes twenty-six and negative ninety, reaching its highest point around May. The figure is located beneath Hydra and is bordered by constellations such as Lupus, Musca, and Crux. Observers can identify it by the bright stars Rigil Kentaurus and Hadar, which serve as the Southern Pointers toward the Southern Cross. The constellation contains the notable globular cluster Omega Centauri, which appears as a hazy fourth-magnitude star to the naked eye.
cards.mythology: In Greek mythology, the figure is often associated with Chiron, the son of Chronos and Philyra, who was known as the wisest and most just of his race. Unlike the threatening Sagittarius, he was imagined as having a mild and noble look and was a renowned instructor of heroes in music, medicine, and astronomy. Another tradition identifies the constellation as Pholos, the hospitable centaur who was transformed into the sky by Hercules. Aratus noted that the figure ever seems to stretch his right hand towards the Altar while firmly grasping another sign called the Beast.

quotes.text: The Centaur's arrow ready seems to pierce Some enemy; far forth his bow is bent Into the blue of heaven.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Centaurus

quotes.text: He was imagined as of mild and noble look, very different from the threatening aspect of the centaur Sagittarius; and Saint Clement of Alexandria wrote of him that he first led mortals to righteousness.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Centaurus

quotes.text: He ever seems to stretch his right hand towards the round Altar, but though his hand is drawn and firmly grasped another sign – the Beast, for so men of old have named it.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Cepheus
cards.summary: Cepheus is a deep northern constellation representing a king of Aethiopia in Greek mythology. It was one of the 48 figures listed by the astronomer Ptolemy in the second century and remains one of the 88 modern constellations. The figure is often depicted in royal robes and is described as being like one who stretches forth both hands.
cards.howToFind: Cepheus is located in the northern sky near the pole, bordered by constellations such as Cassiopeia, Draco, and Ursa Minor. A naked-eye observer can identify the king's head by a triangle formed by the stars Delta, Epsilon, and Zeta, while the stars Alderamin, Alfirk, and Errai mark other parts of the figure. It is highest in the sky at 9pm during October and is fully visible from latitudes between 90 degrees north and 2 degrees south.
cards.mythology: In Greek mythology, Cepheus was the king of Aethiopia and the father of Andromeda. He was connected to the Argonautic expedition and was considered the son of Belos, who was credited as the inventor of stellar science. Aratus describes him as a member of a hapless family set in the heavens because they were near akin to Zeus. Some traditions identify the figure as the aged Nereus, while others associate it with the Babylonian myth of the son of Belos.

quotes.text: Kepheus is like one who stretches forth both hands.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Cepheus

quotes.text: Cepheus himself is set behind the Bear Cynosura, like to one that stretches out both his hands. From her tail-tip to both his feet stretches a measure equal to that from foot to foot.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Cepheus is an inconspicuous constellation, but evidently was highly regarded in early times as the father of the Royal Family, and his story well known in Greek literature of the 5th century before Christ.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Cepheus

cards.name: Cetus
cards.summary: Cetus is a large constellation representing a ferocious sea monster or whale, often associated with the Greek legend of Perseus. It was identified at least as early as the days of Aratus and was likely known on the Euphrates long before that era. The figure is situated in a region of the sky populated by other water-related constellations like Aquarius, Pisces, and Eridanus.
cards.howToFind: Cetus is one of the most extended sky figures, visible between latitudes 64 and -80 and highest in November. An irregular pentagon of stars including Menkar and Kaffaljidhma marks the head directly under Aries, while the body stretches toward the River Eridanus. The star Diphda marks the southern branch of the tail, and the famous variable star Mira is located in the monster's neck.
cards.mythology: In Greek mythology, this creature was the sea monster sent to devour Andromeda, but it was turned to stone when Perseus showed it the head of Medusa. Some traditions suggest the figure was originally the Euphratean Tiamat. Biblical interpreters later identified the constellation as the whale that swallowed Jonah or the Leviathan mentioned in the Book of Job.

quotes.text: The south wind brings her foe The Ocean beast.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Cetus

quotes.text: Andromeda, though she cowers a good way off, is pressed by the rush of the mighty Monster of the Sea. For her path lies under the blast of Thracian Boreas, but the South wind drives against her, beneath the Ram and the Pair of Fishes, the hateful Monster, Cetus, set as he is a little above the Starry River.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Chamaeleon
cards.summary: Chamaeleon is a small and unimportant constellation located in the deep southern sky. It represents the chameleon lizard and was first defined at the end of the 16th century.
cards.howToFind: This constellation is visible to observers between latitudes 8 and -90 degrees and is highest in the sky during April. It is situated below Carina and is separated from the south pole by Octans, with other neighbors including Apus, Mensa, Musca, and Volans. While it has no named stars in Western tradition, some of its components form a pattern known in China as Seaou Tow, a small Measure or Dipper.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this constellation. It was first published and figured by Bayer among his new constellations based on observations by navigators of the 16th century. Julius Schiller later attempted to change its character by combining it with Apus and Musca to represent the biblical Eve.

quotes.text: It was first published and figured by Bayer among his new constellations from observations by navigators of the preceding century. Pontanus, in Chilmead's Treatise, included it with Musca as "the Chamaelon with the flie";

cards.name: Circinus
cards.summary: Circinus is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky representing a drafting tool used for drawing circles. It was first defined in 1756 by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
cards.howToFind: Observers can locate this figure in the southern sky between latitudes 20 and -90 degrees, where it is highest at 9pm around June. It lies close to the front feet of the Centaur, south from Lupus and Norma, and also shares borders with Apus, Musca, and Triangulum Australe. The constellation contains the star Xami and a Cepheid variable visible with the unaided eye.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient mythology associated with this constellation. It was formed by La Caille, who appropriately associated it with the drafting tool known as the Pair of Compasses.

quotes.text: Circinus, the Pair of Compasses, formed by La Caille, lies close to the front feet of the Centaur, south from Lupus and Norma, its inventor appropriately associating it with the latter.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Circinus

quotes.text: Its name is Latin for compass, referring to the drafting tool used for drawing circles.

cards.name: Columba
cards.summary: Columba is a faint constellation designated in the late sixteenth century that represents a dove. Its name is Latin for dove and it was originally formed from the southwestern outliers of Canis Major.
cards.howToFind: Columba is located south of Canis Major and Lepus, lying on the same meridian as the stars in Orions Belt. To identify the figure, look for the stars Phact and Wazn which represent the back of the bird. The constellation is fully visible between latitudes 47 and -90 and is highest in the evening sky around February.
cards.mythology: Columba was introduced by Petrus Plancius in the 16th century and later published by Royer. It is regarded as Noahs Dove, the attendant to the nearby constellation of the Ship which represents Noahs Ark. Some stars in the figure were consecrated to the Appeased Deity and the retiring of the waters in the time of the Deluge.

quotes.text: It was made up from the southwestern outliers of Canis Major, near to the Ship, — Noah's Ark, — and so was regarded as the attendant Dove.

quotes.text: Others underneath the hunted Hare, All very dim and nameless roll along.

cards.name: Coma Berenices
cards.summary: Coma Berenices is an ancient asterism and modern constellation representing Berenice's Hair. It was introduced in the third century BC by Conon of Samos and is the only modern constellation named after a historic person.
cards.howToFind: The constellation lies between Leo and Boötes, situated southwest from Cor Caroli. Observers can identify it by the star Diadem and a cloudy condensation of stars that appears like "gossamers spangled with dewdrops" were entangled there. It is visible in both hemispheres and reaches its highest point in the evening sky around May.
cards.mythology: The constellation honors Queen Berenice II of Egypt, who sacrificed her long hair as a votive offering in the temple of Arsinoë Aphrodite. When the tresses were stolen, Conon of Samos consoled the royal pair by claiming the amber hair had been placed in the sky. Other traditions have associated the group with Ariadne's Hair, a Distaff held by the Virgin, or a Pond into which a frightened Gazelle leaped.

quotes.text: It was the happy invention of this constellation by Conon that consoled the royal pair after the theft of the tresses from the temple of Arsinoë Aphrodite at Zephyrium. Some versions of the story turned the lady's hair into a hair-star, or comet.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Coma Berenices

quotes.text: the consecrated spoils of Berenice's yellow head, which the divine Venus placed, a new constellation, among the ancient ones, preceding the slow Boötes, who sinks late and reluctantly into the deep ocean.

cards.name: Corona Australis
cards.summary: Corona Australis is a small constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere whose Latin name means southern crown. It is one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy and was seen by the Ancient Greeks as a wreath. Other cultures have identified the pattern as a turtle, a tent, or even an ostrich nest.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find this figure near the waist of Sagittarius on the edge of the Milky Way. It is highest in the sky around August and is fully visible to anyone between 44 degrees north and 90 degrees south latitude. The constellation is composed of stars including Alqubba, Meridiana, and Qedty, which form a shape that has been described as a heart-shaped object or a circle roll without a name.
cards.mythology: Ancient Greeks associated this wreath with the nearby figures of Sagittarius or Centaurus. Some classical poets believed it was the crown Bacchus placed in the sky to honor his mother Semele, while others saw it as the wheel of Ixion. It has also been identified as the crown of eternal life from the New Testament or the diadem of Solomon. One tradition suggests it represents a wreath commemorating the fivefold victory of Corinna over Pindar in a poetical contest.

quotes.text: other few, Below the Archer under his forefeet, Led round in circle roll without a name.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Corona Australis

quotes.text: The Ancient Greeks saw Corona Australis as a wreath rather than a crown and associated it with Sagittarius or Centaurus.

cards.name: Corona Borealis
cards.summary: Corona Borealis is a small constellation in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere whose brightest stars form a semicircular arc. Its Latin name means northern crown, and it was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy. It generally represents the crown given by the god Dionysus to the Cretan princess Ariadne.
cards.howToFind: Look for an almost perfect semicircle of stars located twenty degrees northeast of the bright star Arcturus. The constellation is situated between Boötes, Hercules, and Serpens, and is highest in the sky around July. Its figure is marked by the central star Alphecca, also known as the Pearl of the Crown, along with Nusakan, Baltesha, and Guansuo.
cards.mythology: In classical lore, this figure is the crown worn by Ariadne, the daughter of King Minos of Crete. After she was deserted by Theseus at Naxos, she became the wife of Dionysus, who set her crown in the heavens as a memorial. Other traditions have identified the pattern as a broken platter, a pauper's bowl, or the crown placed by Ahasuerus upon the head of Esther.

quotes.text: Here too that Crown, which glorious Dionysus set to be memorial of the dead Ariadne, wheels beneath the back of the toil-spent Phantom.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Still her sign is seen in heaven, And midst the glittering symbols of the sky The starry crown of Ariadne glides.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Corona Borealis

quotes.text: One plac'd i' th' front above the rest displays A vigorous light, and darts surprising rays — The Monument of the forsaken Maid.

cards.name: Corvus
cards.summary: Corvus is a small constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere that depicts a raven perched on the back of Hydra the water snake. It was one of the forty-eight constellations listed by the second-century astronomer Ptolemy. The name of the constellation means raven in Latin.
cards.howToFind: Observers can identify this constellation by its four brightest stars, Gienah, Kraz, Algorab, and Alchiba, which form a distinctive quadrilateral or cross-shape. It is located near the constellations Crater, Hydra, and Virgo. The figure is fully visible between latitudes sixty-six and negative ninety, reaching its highest point in the night sky around May.
cards.mythology: In Greek mythology, the bird was sacred to Phoebus Apollo, who assumed its shape during the conflict between the gods and the giants. One legend says the raven was originally silver but was turned black by Apollo for reporting the unfaithfulness of Coronis. Another story claims the bird was sent for water but loitered at a fig tree until the fruit ripened; it returned with a water snake in its claws and a lie to explain the delay. As punishment, it was fixed in the sky with the Cup and the Snake, doomed to thirst while the Hydra guards the water.

quotes.text: Another constellation trails beyond, which men call the Hydra. Like a living creature it winds afar its coiling form. Its head comes beneath the middle of the Crab, its coil beneath the body of the Lion, and its tail hangs above the Centaur himself. Midway on its coiling form is set the Crater, and at the tip the figure of a Raven that seems to peck at the coil.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Continuata loco tria sidera, Corvus et Anguis, Et medius Crater inter utrumque jacet;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Corvus

quotes.text: Hither, monster, come not back; And — to match thy disposition — Henceforth be thy plumage black!
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Corvus

cards.name: Crater
cards.summary: Crater is a small constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere that represents a cup or goblet. One of the forty-eight figures listed by Ptolemy, it is depicted as being perched on the back of Hydra the water snake.
cards.howToFind: Crater is best seen in April when it is highest in the sky. It is located south of Leo and Virgo, appearing as a partly annular form opening to the northwest. To find it, look for the orange star Alkes, which sits at the base of the cup just westward from Corvus.
cards.mythology: In Greek tradition, this figure was the goblet of Apollo. It has also been associated with the wine cup of Bacchus and the cup of Medea, which links it to the Argonautic myths. Later Christian interpretations by Caesius identified it as the cup of Christ's Passion or the stone water pots of Cana.

quotes.text: Midway on its coiling form is set the Crater, and at the tip the figure of a Raven that seems to peck at the coil.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: the generous Bowl Of Bacchus flows, and chears the thirsty Pole.

quotes.text: Wise ancients knew when Crater rose to sight, Nile's fertile deluge had attained its height;

cards.name: Crux
cards.summary: Crux is a small but easily distinguished constellation of the southern sky representing a cross. Although it is the smallest of all 88 modern constellations, it is centered on four bright stars and has attained high cultural significance in many Southern Hemisphere nations.
cards.howToFind: Crux is located on the southern end of the Milky Way's visible band, surrounded on three sides by Centaurus and bordering Musca to the south. An observer can identify the cross-shaped asterism by its four main stars, Acrux, Mimosa, Gacrux, and Imai, though the fifth star Ginan somewhat interferes with the regularity of the figure. It is fully visible between latitudes 26 and -90 and is highest in the evening sky around May.
cards.mythology: Crux was unknown to the ancients as a separate figure, as its stars were originally noted by Ptolemy as part of the hind feet of the Centaur. Its invention as a distinct constellation is often attributed to Royer in 1679, though it appeared on globes as early as 1592 and was described by voyagers like Vespucci and Pigafetta. A native Australian legend describes the nearby Coal-sack as an Emu lying in wait at the foot of a tree represented by the stars of the Cross.

quotes.text: The two great stars, which mark the summit and the foot of the Cross, having nearly the same right ascension, it follows that the constellation is almost perpendicular at the moment when it passes the meridian.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Crux

quotes.text: It is a time piece, which advances very regularly nearly four minutes a day, and no other group of stars affords to the naked eye an observation of time so easily made.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Crux

quotes.text: Crux lies in the Milky Way, — here a brilliant but narrow stream three or four degrees wide, — and is noticeable from its compression as well as its form, being only 6° in extent from north to south, and less in width
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Crux

cards.name: Cygnus
cards.summary: Cygnus is a northern constellation positioned on the plane of the Milky Way that represents a swan. It was catalogued by Ptolemy in the 2nd century and contains the recognizable Northern Cross asterism.
cards.howToFind: In September, look for the bright star Deneb marking the tail and Albireo at the beak. The figure forms a cross with Sadr at the center, located between Draco and Pegasus. It is fully visible for observers between latitudes 90 and -29 degrees.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, the figure represents a swan associated with Leda or the brother of Phaethon who was transformed and placed in the sky. It was also identified as the musician Orpheus, situated near his Lyre. Ancient Arabic traditions often depicted the group as a hen, while later observers saw it as the Cross of Calvary.

quotes.text: For verily in heaven there is outspread a glittering Bird. Wreathed in mist is the Bird, but yet the parts above him are rough with stars, not very large, yet not obscure.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Like a bird in joyous flight, with fair weather it glides to the west, with the tip of its right wing outstretched towards the right hand of Cepheus, and by its left wing is hung in the heavens the prancing Horse.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Cygnus usually is shown in full flight down the Milky Way, the Stream of Heaven, "uppoised on gleaming wings"; but old drawings have it apparently just springing from the ground.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Cygnus

cards.name: Delphinus
cards.summary: Delphinus is a small constellation in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere representing a dolphin. It was one of the original 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy and is the Latin version for the Greek word for dolphin.
cards.howToFind: Located east of Aquila on the edge of the Milky Way, this figure is highest in the sky around September. A naked-eye observer can identify its distinctive asterism of five stars, including Sualocin, Rotanev, and Aldulfin, which symbolize a dolphin with four stars representing the body and one the tail. It is bordered by other figures such as Pegasus, Aquarius, and Sagitta.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, the dolphin was placed in the stars for inducing Amphitrite to become the wife of Neptune. Another favorite story identifies it as the creature that rescued the musician Arion during a voyage. It has also been associated with the pirate-pilot Acetes who protected Bacchus, and in later popular tradition, it is known as Job's Coffin.

quotes.text: Over Aegoceros floats the Dolphin with few bright stars and body wreathed in mist, but four brilliants adorn him, set side by side in pairs.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: The Glory of the Flood and of the Stars.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Delphinus

quotes.text: a marine animal friendly to man, attendant upon ships to save the drowning sailors.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Delphinus

cards.name: Dorado
cards.summary: Dorado is a constellation in the Southern Sky that represents the mahi-mahi, a large fish of the tropical seas. It was named in the late 16th century and was first published by Bayer among his new southern figures.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Dorado in the southern heavens, where it is highest at 9pm around January. It is fully visible between latitudes 20 and -90 degrees, situated near the constellations Volans, Pictor, and Mensa. The figure contains most of the Large Magellanic Cloud and its head marks the south pole of the ecliptic, a point once known as the Polus Doradinalis.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this constellation as it was introduced in the late 16th century. While it is named for the mahi-mahi, it has also been depicted as a swordfish under the alternative title Xiphias. Caesius once combined its stars with the Flying Fish to form the Old Testament figure of Abel the Just.

quotes.text: The word is from the Spanish, and refers not to our little exotic cyprinoid, but to the large coryphaena of the tropical seas, of changing colors at death.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Dorado

quotes.text: Dorado contains most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, the remainder being in the constellation Mensa. The South Ecliptic pole also lies within this constellation.

cards.name: Draco
cards.summary: Draco is a large constellation in the far northern sky representing a dragon. It was one of the original forty-eight constellations listed by Ptolemy and contains the north pole of the ecliptic.
cards.howToFind: Draco is circumpolar from northern latitudes and is highest at 9pm around July. An observer can find its winding figure between the two Bears, with its head marked by the stars Eltanin and Rastaban near the constellation Lyra. The body meanders past Ursa Minor and Ursa Major, featuring stars such as Thuban, Altais, and Aldhibah.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, this was the snake snatched by Minerva from the giants and whirled to the sky. Other myths identify it as the monster killed by Cadmus at the fount of Mars or the dragon Ladon that guarded the golden fruit in the Garden of the Hesperides. Some traditions see it as the dragon Tiamat overcome by the kneeling sun-god, while others identify it as a sea monster or the serpent that tempted Eve.

quotes.text: Between them, as it were the branch of a river, circles in wondrous way the Dragon, winding infinite around and about; on either side of his coil are borne along the Bears, that shun evermore the blue sea.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: With vast convolutions Draco holds Th' ecliptic axis in his scaly folds. O'er half the skies his neck enormous rears, And with immense meanders parts the Bears.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Draco

quotes.text: Ladon, from the prominent river of Arcadia, or, more probably, the estuary bounding the Garden of the Hesperides, which, in the ordinary version of the story, Draco guarded, "the emblem of eternal vigilance in that it never set."
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Draco

cards.name: Equuleus
cards.summary: Equuleus is a faint constellation located just north of the celestial equator and is the second smallest of the modern constellations. Its name is Latin for little horse, a foal, and it was one of the forty-eight constellations listed by the second century astronomer Ptolemy. It represents the upper part of an animal figure, often described as a bust or the Horse's Head.
cards.howToFind: Equuleus is located half-way between the head of Pegasus and the Dolphin. Observers can identify it by a small trapezium of stars including Kitalpha and Tepennekhet. It is highest at nine pm around September and is visible to observers between latitudes of ninety degrees north and seventy-eight degrees south.
cards.mythology: No certain tale or historie is delivered thereof, by what means it came into heaven, as the constellation was named by almost no writer except Ptolemy. Some mythologists later associated it with Celeris, the brother of Pegasus, or Cyllarus, a horse given to Pollux by Juno. It has also been identified as the creature struck by Neptune's trident during his contest with Minerva.

quotes.text: This constellation was named of almost no writer, saving Ptolomee and Alfonsus who followith Ptolomee, and therefore no certain tale or historie is delivered thereof, by what means it came into heaven;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Equuleus

quotes.text: Equuleus is a faint constellation located just north of the celestial equator. Its name is Latin for "little horse", a foal. It was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd century astronomer Ptolemy, and remains one of the 88 modern constellations.

quotes.text: Ptolemy catalogued it as Ἵππου Προτομή, this last word equivalent to our Bust for the upper part of an animal figure; but with later astronomers it was Equus primus and prior, as preceding Pegasus in rising;

cards.name: Eridanus
cards.summary: Eridanus is a vast constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere that is represented as a river. It was one of the original forty-eight constellations listed by Ptolemy and remains the sixth largest of the modern figures. The name has been historically associated with various earthly waters, including the Po River and the Nile.
cards.howToFind: The constellation is a long, winding stream that begins near the star Rigel in Orion and meanders past the paws of Cetus. It is highest in the evening sky around January and is fully visible to observers between latitudes thirty-two and negative ninety. Its figure is defined by stars such as Cursa, Zaurak, and Rana, ending far to the south at the bright Achernar.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, this is the starry Stream of many tears where Phaethon was hurled by Jove after his disastrous attempt to drive the chariot of the sun. His sisters, the Heliades, wept for him until their tears turned to amber in the water. Some ancient authors instead identified the figure as the Nile, the only great river known to flow from the south toward the north.

quotes.text: For this a remnant of Eridanos, That stream of tears, 'neath the gods' feet is borne.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Eridanus

quotes.text: The winding River will straightway sink in fair flowing ocean at the coming of Scorpion, whose rising puts to flight even the mighty Orion.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Like the stars of heaven he shall shine; like the River of Night he shall flow;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Eridanus

cards.name: Fornax
cards.summary: Fornax is a constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere whose name is Latin for furnace. It was named by French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille in 1756 and is one of the 88 modern constellations.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Fornax within the southern bend of the celestial river Eridanus, also sharing borders with Cetus, Phoenix, and Sculptor. Look for the star Dalim, which is the lucida of the figure. It is best seen in December and is fully visible to anyone located between 50 degrees north and 90 degrees south latitude.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this constellation. It was formed by La Caille from stars in the southern sky and was originally called Fornax Chemica, or Fornax Chymiae, the Chemical Furnace. The Chinese know it as Tien Yu, Heaven's Temporary Granary.

quotes.text: Fornax Chemica, or Fornax Chymiae, the Chemical Furnace, was formed by La Caille from stars within the southern bend of the River; but modern astronomers, by whom it is still recognized, have abbreviated the title to Fornax.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Fornax

quotes.text: Bode changed the early name in 1782 to Apparatus chemicus, and translated it as the Chemische Apparat, Chymische Ofen, and l'Apparat Chimique, an alteration in honor of the celebrated chemist Antoine Laurent Lavoisier.

cards.name: Gemini
cards.summary: Gemini is a prominent zodiac constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere representing two brothers. Its name is Latin for twins, and it was one of the original forty-eight figures catalogued by the astronomer Ptolemy in the 2nd century.
cards.howToFind: Gemini is highest in the sky around February and is fully visible between latitudes 90 and -54 degrees. To find the figure, look for the two bright stars Castor and Pollux, which mark the heads of the twins above the setting Orion in April. The constellation is located between Cancer and Auriga, with other figure stars like Alhena and Mebsuta forming the bodies of the twins.
cards.mythology: In Greek mythology, the constellation represents the twins Castor and Pollux, the sons of Leda. Castor was considered the mortal horseman and son of Tyndarus, while Pollux was the immortal pugilist and son of Zeus. They were placed in the sky by Jove in reward for their brotherly love and were often invoked by sailors as protectors who delivered stricken barks from wreck during wintry tempests.

quotes.text:
Tender Gemini in strict embrace
Stand clos'd and smiling in each other's Face;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Gemini

quotes.text:
So Leda's twins, bright-shining, at their beck
Oft have delivered stricken barks from wreck.

quotes.text: Beneath the head of Helice are the Twins; beneath her waist is the Crab; beneath her hind feet the Lion brightly shines. There is the Sun’s hottest summer path.

cards.name: Grus
cards.summary: Grus is a southern constellation representing the crane, a type of bird. It was conceived by Petrus Plancius using observations from Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman, first appearing on a celestial globe in 1598.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find this figure south of Piscis Austrinus, where its stars form a gentle curve. The star Alnair marks the body of the bird and is conspicuous southwest from Fomalhaut during October evenings. Other primary stars include Tiaki in the left wing and Aldhanab marking the eye. It is fully visible for observers between latitudes 33 and -90 degrees.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this figure as it was a modern invention of the late 16th century. Horapollo of Alexandria noted that the crane was an Egyptian symbol for a star-observer due to its high flight. While Julius Schiller saw the figure as Aaron the High Priest, the Spaniards once called it the Flamingo, describing it as striking with its bill at the Southern Fish.

quotes.text: Horapollo, the grammarian of Alexandria, about A.D. 400, tells us that the crane was the symbol of a star-observer in Egypt, presumably from its high flight as described in our motto.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Grus

quotes.text: The constellations Grus, Pavo, Phoenix and Tucana are collectively known as the "Southern Birds".

quotes.text: The Spaniards call it Flamengo: and it is described with the wings spread abroad, and as it were striking with its bill at the South Fish, in that part where he boweth himselfe.

cards.name: Hercules
cards.summary: Hercules is a large constellation named after the Roman hero adapted from the Greek Heracles. It was one of the forty-eight constellations listed by Ptolemy and is the fifth-largest of the modern constellations. The figure is one of the oldest in the sky, though it was not known to the first Greek astronomers as the hero we recognize today.
cards.howToFind: Hercules is highest in the sky around July and is fully visible between latitudes ninety and negative thirty-eight. To find it, look between the head of Ophiuchus and the constellation Draco, where the figure is described as having its right foot planted on the twisting Serpent's head. The constellation contains no stars brighter than magnitude two point five, but its primary figure stars include Kornephoros, Sarin, and Nüchuang, with the star Rasalgethi marking the head.
cards.mythology: Early Greek astronomers like Eudoxos and Hipparchos knew this figure only as the Kneeling One or the Phantom, a toiling man whose specific task was unknown. Eratosthenes was the first to identify the figure as Hercules standing upon the dragon Draco. Modern students of mythology suggest the figure may have originated from the sun-god Izhdubar in Euphratean myths or the sea-god Melkarth in ancient Phoenicia. The constellation has also been associated with Prometheus in chains, the leaper Saltator, and the biblical Adam.

quotes.text:
. . . like a toiling man, revolves
A form. Of it can no one clearly speak,
Nor to what toil he is attached; but, simply,
Kneeler they call him. Laboring on his knees,
Like one who sinks he seems; . . .
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Hercules

quotes.text: Right there in its orbit wheels a Phantom form, like to a man that strives at a task. That sign no man knows how to read clearly, nor what task he is bent, but men simply call him On His Knees.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text:
Conscious of his shame
A constellation kneels without a name.

cards.name: Horologium
cards.summary: Horologium is a faint constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere that represents a pendulum clock with a second hand. It was first described by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1756.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find this constellation in the southern sky between latitudes 22 degrees North and 90 degrees South, reaching its highest point in December. It lies to the eastward of the star Achernar in Eridanus and north of Hydrus, sharing borders with Caelum, Dorado, and Reticulum.
cards.mythology: There is no myth associated with this figure as it was a modern invention. Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille introduced it in the 18th century as Horologium Oscillatorium, the Pendulum Clock.

quotes.text: Horologium Oscillatorium, the Pendulum Clock, lies to the eastward of Achernar, — α of Eridanus, — and north of Hydrus.

cards.name: Hydra
cards.summary: Hydra is the largest and longest of the modern constellations, commonly represented as a water snake that straddles the celestial equator. It was included among the forty-eight constellations listed by Ptolemy and is sometimes associated with the Dragon of Aetes from the Argonautic legends.
cards.howToFind: Hydra winds across the sky from Cancer to Libra and Centaurus, reaching its highest point in April. An observer can identify its head below the middle of Cancer, while its long body coils beneath Leo and carries the constellations Crater and Corvus on its back. The figure is marked by the solitary orange star Alphard and other named stars like Naga, Ashlesha, and Zhang.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, the figure is often shown with a cup and a raven on its back; the snake prevents the bird from drinking as punishment for the raven's delay in serving Apollo. Some ancient accounts identified it as the dragon that guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides. Other traditions have viewed the constellation as a representative of the River Nile or the biblical Flood.

quotes.text: Another constellation trails beyond, which men call the Hydra. Like a living creature it winds afar its coiling form. Its head comes beneath the middle of the Crab, its coil beneath the body of the Lion, and its tail hangs above the Centaur himself.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Close by the Serpent spreads; whose winding Spires With ordered stars resemble scaly Fires.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Hydra

quotes.text: Hydra, the Water-snake, is the French Hydre, the German Grosse Wasserschlange, and the Italian Idra, and may be classed among the Argonautic constellations, as it was said to represent the Dragon of Aetes.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Hydra

cards.name: Hydrus
cards.summary: Hydrus is a small constellation in the deep southern sky that represents a male water snake. It was one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the late sixteenth century.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Hydrus in the deep southern sky, where it is highest at nine in the evening during December. It lies between Horologium and Tucana, with its head adjoining Octans and its tail almost reaching the star Achernar in Eridanus. The constellation is fully visible for those located between latitudes eight degrees and negative ninety degrees.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient myth associated with this figure as it was introduced by Petrus Plancius in 1597. Its name means "male water snake", distinguishing it from the much larger and more ancient constellation Hydra which represents a female water snake. Julius Schiller later used these stars to form his biblical constellation Raphael.

quotes.text: Its name means "male water snake", as opposed to Hydra, a much larger constellation that represents a female water snake. It remains below the horizon for most Northern Hemisphere observers.
quotes.source: Wikipedia: Hydrus

quotes.text: The 2.7‑magnitude lucida β, in the tail, is of remarkably clear yellow hue, and the nearest conspicuous star to the south pole, although 12° distant.

cards.name: Indus
cards.summary: Indus represents the Indian and was first professionally surveyed by Europeans in the 1590s. It was mapped on a globe by Petrus Plancius and later included in the 1603 sky atlas Uranometria by Johann Bayer. The figure is often described as an inhabitant of Madagascar or the East Indies.
cards.howToFind: The constellation is located in the southern sky between Grus and Pavo, and it sits south of Microscopium. It is best viewed in September and is fully visible for observers south of 15 degrees latitude. Its chief stars form a triangular shape that is elongated from north to south.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient myth associated with this constellation as it was introduced in the late 16th century. While it is generally supposed to represent a typical American Indian, early illustrators drew it as a nude figure holding arrows in both hands but no bow. Julius Schiller later attempted to re-imagine the stars as the patriarch Job by joining them with the constellation Pavo.

quotes.text: It is one of Bayer's new constellations, south of the Microscope, between Grus and Pavo, and, although generally supposed to represent a typical American Indian, its publisher drew it as a far more civilized character, yet nude, with arrows in both hands, but no bow.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Indus

cards.name: Lacerta
cards.summary: Lacerta is a small and faint constellation whose name is Latin for lizard. It was defined in 1687 by the astronomer Johannes Hevelius, who selected this figure because there was not space for any of a different shape.
cards.howToFind: Look for this constellation between Cygnus, Cassiopeia, and Andromeda on the northern celestial sphere. Its brightest stars, including Stellio and Alsamaka, form a "W" shape similar to that of Cassiopeia. It is highest in the sky around October and is fully visible for observers between ninety degrees north and thirty-four degrees south latitude.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient mythology for this figure as it was introduced in the seventeenth century by Hevelius. He originally drew a strange weasel-built creature with a curly tail and gave it the alternative title of Stellio, referring to a newt with star-like dorsal spots. Before the Lizard was established, other astronomers attempted to place the Sceptre and Hand of Justice or the Frederici Honores in this region, but these figures were eventually forgotten.

quotes.text: This inconspicuous constellation was formed by Hevelius from outlying stars between Cygnus and Andromeda, this special figure having been selected because there was not space for any of a different shape.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Lacerta

quotes.text: Its brightest stars form a "W" shape similar to that of Cassiopeia, and it is thus sometimes referred to as 'Little Cassiopeia'.

cards.name: Leo
cards.summary: Leo is a prominent zodiacal constellation in the Northern celestial hemisphere that represents the Nemean Lion. It is one of the original forty-eight constellations described by Ptolemy and is easily recognized by a shape reminiscent of a crouching lion.
cards.howToFind: Leo is located between Cancer to the west and Virgo to the east, positioned beneath the hind feet of Ursa Major. Observers can identify the figure by the distinctive Sickle pattern forming the lion's mane and head, with the bright star Regulus marking the handle. The constellation is highest in the evening sky around April and is fully visible between latitudes eighty-four degrees North and fifty-six degrees South.
cards.mythology: In Greek mythology, this constellation represents the Nemean Lion, a monstrous creature killed by the hero Heracles as one of his twelve labors. The lion was said to have originally come from the moon before its earthly stay. Some ancient traditions also identified the figure as a transformation of the god Bacchus, who frequently wore a lion's skin. Because the sun once reached the summer solstice among these stars, the constellation has been associated with fire and heat across many cultures.

quotes.text: Leo is one of the constellations of the zodiac, between Cancer, the Crab, to the west and Virgo, the Maiden, to the east. It is located in the Northern celestial hemisphere.
quotes.source: Wikipedia: Leo (constellation)

quotes.text: Beneath the head of Helice are the Twins; beneath her waist is the Crab; beneath her hind feet the Lion brightly shines. There is the Sun’s hottest summer path.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: In Greek and Roman myth this was respectively Λέων and Leo, representing the Nemean Lion, originally from the moon, and, after his earthly stay, carried back to the heavens with his slayer Hercules, where he became the poet's Nemeaeus
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Leo
