cards.name: Leo Minor
cards.summary: Leo Minor is a small and faint constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere. Its name is Latin for "the smaller lion", in contrast to Leo, the larger lion.
cards.howToFind: Observers can locate this figure between Ursa Major to the north and Leo to the south. It appears as a long triangle with a fainter line to the south, containing the star Praecipua. The constellation is highest at 9pm around April and is visible between latitudes -48 and 90.
cards.mythology: Leo Minor was not regarded as a separate constellation by classical astronomers; it was designated by Johannes Hevelius in 1687. Hevelius formed it from stars between the greater Lion and Bear because he felt it was of the same nature as those figures. The Chinese alternatively saw these stars as an Inner Screen or a State Chariot.

quotes.text: It was formed by Hevelius from eighteen stars between the greater Lion and Bear, in a long triangle with a fainter line to the south, and thus named because he said it was "of the same nature" as these adjoining constellations.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Leo Minor

quotes.text: Aratos is supposed to have alluded to these "ungrouped, unnamed" stars under the hind paws of Ursa Major; and Ptolemy had some of them among the ἀμόρφωτοι of his Λέων.

cards.name: Lepus
cards.summary: Lepus is a constellation located just south of the celestial equator, immediately below Orion. Its name is Latin for hare, and it is frequently depicted as a creature being chased by the hunter Orion or his dogs.
cards.howToFind: To find the Hare, look directly south of Orion and westward from the constellation of the Hound. The figure is marked by the stars Arneb, Nihal, Ping, Bade, and Darlugal, and is highest in the sky around 9pm in January. It is fully visible to any observer between the latitudes of sixty-three degrees north and ninety degrees south.
cards.mythology: Ancient Greek lore describes the Hare as being placed in the heavens to be close to its hunter, Orion. Aratus characterizes the constellation as the Hare pursued continually through all time, while Sirius follows closely behind to eye the setting creature. Some ancient traditions associated the figure with the moon, while other cultures saw it as a shed or the Boat of Osiris.

quotes.text: Beneath both feet of Orion is the Hare pursued continually through all time, while Seirius behind for ever borne as in pursuit. Close behind he rises and as he sets he eyes the setting Hare.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: The problem which perplexed the ancients, why the Mighty-hunter and his Dog should pursue the most timid of creatures, is solved when we recognize that Orion was originally a solar type, and that the Hare is almost universally a lunar type;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Lepus

quotes.text: Now the other stars are grouped in clear figures and brightly shine, but those beneath the hunted Hare are all clad in mist and nameless in their course.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Libra
cards.summary: Libra is a zodiac constellation in the Southern celestial hemisphere whose name is Latin for weighing scales. It is a fairly faint figure that was once considered a distinct portion of the Scorpion known as the Claws.
cards.howToFind: Libra lies between Virgo to the west and Scorpius to the east. It is fully visible between latitudes sixty and negative ninety, reaching its highest point in the evening around June. An observer can identify its central trapezoid formed by the stars Zubeneschamali, Zubenelgenubi, Zubenelhakrabi, and Brachium.
cards.mythology: The early Greeks did not associate these stars with a balance, instead calling them the Claws of the Scorpion. The Romans claimed to have added the Scales to the original eleven signs during the formation of the Julian calendar in 46 B.C. Some associate the figure with the goddess of justice, Astraea, or with the equality of day and night because the sun once entered the sign at the autumnal equinox. In other traditions, it has been identified as an ancient altar, a lamp, or even the chariot of Pluto.

quotes.text: Toward the Crown leans the Serpent’s jaw, but beneath his coiling form seek thou for the mighty Claws; they are scant of light and nowise brilliant.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Then Day and Night are weigh'd in Libra's Scale Equal a while,

quotes.text: the Scorpion having contracted his claws to make room for his neighbour.

cards.name: Lupus
cards.summary: Lupus is a constellation of the mid-Southern Sky whose name is Latin for wolf. It was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy, though it was mostly considered an asterism associated with the nearby Centaurus.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Lupus south of Libra and Scorpius and east of the Centaur. It is fully visible between latitudes 35 and -90, reaching its highest point in the evening around June. The figure contains the star Uridim and is described as the Wild-beast which the Centaur's right hand holds.
cards.mythology: The Greeks and Romans did not specially designate these stars as a wolf, referring to the figure merely as a Wild Animal or the Beast. Aratus described it as an offering to the gods held by the Centaur, while Eratosthenes suggested it was a Wine-skin. Some mythologists later associated it with Lycaon, the man changed into a wolf, while others identified it as the animal to which Jacob likened Benjamin.

quotes.text: He ever seems to stretch his right hand towards the round Altar, but though his hand is drawn and firmly grasped another sign – the Beast, for so men of old have named it.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Lynx
cards.summary: Lynx is a faint constellation in the northern sky named after the animal. It was introduced in the late 17th century by Johannes Hevelius and its brightest stars form a zigzag line.
cards.howToFind: The constellation is highest in the sky around March and is fully visible between latitudes 90 and -28 degrees. Observers can find it due north from the star Castor or by looking for the orange giant star Alsciaukat. It is situated among the constellations of Auriga, Camelopardalis, Cancer, Gemini, Leo Minor, and Ursa Major.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient myth associated with this figure as it was introduced by Johannes Hevelius. Hevelius explained that those who would examine the constellation ought to be lynx-eyed because of the insignificance of its components. An alternative name, Tigris, was once used because the many little stars were thought to resemble spots on a tiger.

quotes.text: He used in it nineteen stars, and in explaining the title said that those who would examine the Lynx ought to be lynx-eyed, in which he acknowledged the insignificance of the components.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Lynx

quotes.text: The alternative name, now in disuse, came from the fancied resemblance of the many little stars to spots on the tiger; and the same word was applied by Bartschius in 1624, although as the river Tigris

cards.name: Lyra
cards.summary: Lyra is a small constellation in the Northern Sky that represents the fabled instrument invented by Hermes. It was one of the forty-eight figures listed by Ptolemy and is often depicted as a lyre carried by a vulture or eagle.
cards.howToFind: Lyra is highest in the sky during August and is fully visible between latitudes ninety degrees north and forty-two degrees south. To find it, look for the brilliant star Vega, which forms an equilateral triangle with the stars epsilon and zeta. The figure is bordered by Draco, Hercules, Vulpecula, and Cygnus, and features a small pattern including the stars Sulafat, Sheliak, Jiantai, and Kautoki.
cards.mythology: The constellation represents the first stringed instrument of the Greek bards, which Hermes created by piercing a tortoise shell and adding strings. Hermes gave the lyre to his half-brother Apollo, who later passed it to the musician Orpheus. According to lore, the instrument was placed in the heavens near Hercules to provide a sweet lenimen for his labors.

quotes.text: Yonder, too, is the tiny Tortoise, which, while still beside his cradle, Hermes pierced for stings and bade it be called the Lyre: and he brought it into heaven and set it in front of the unknown Phantom.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Gain'd it Heaven, and still its force appears, As then the Rocks it now draws on the Stars.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Lyra

quotes.text: Decus Phoebi, et dapibus supremi Grata testudo Jovis; O laborum Dulce lenimen;

cards.name: Mensa
cards.summary: Mensa is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere that represents a table. It was one of fourteen constellations drawn up in the 18th century by French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille and originally commemorated Table Mountain.
cards.howToFind: This constellation is a keystone-shaped wedge of sky located near the south celestial pole. It is observable only south of the 5th parallel of the Northern Hemisphere and is highest in the sky around January. Look for it between its neighbours Hydrus, Volans, and Octans, just north of the south pole. The figure contains the star Hoerikwaggo and a portion of the Nubecula Major.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient mythology associated with this figure. Lacaille formed the constellation from stars under the Greater Cloud to honor the Table Mountain back of Cape Town. He chose this name because the mountain which had witnessed his nightly vigils and daily toils also was frequently capped by a cloud.

quotes.text: La Caille, who did so much for our knowledge of the southern heavens, formed the figure from stars under the Greater Cloud, between the poles of the equator and the ecliptic, just north of the polar Octans;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Mons Mensae

quotes.text: Its name is Latin for table, though it originally commemorated Table Mountain and was known as "Mons Mensae".

cards.name: Microscopium
cards.summary: Microscopium is a minor constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere that represents a scientific instrument. It is one of twelve constellations created in the 18th century by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
cards.howToFind: The constellation is best seen in September when it is highest at 9pm. It is located south of Capricornus and west of Piscis Austrinus, and it also borders Sagittarius, Grus, and Indus. Observers can look for the star Aerostaticus within its borders, though its stars are faint and hardly visible from most of the non-tropical Northern Hemisphere.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this figure as it was introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century. However, an earlier figure known as Neper, the Auger, was once described in the same vicinity at the tail of Sagittarius and Capricornus.

quotes.text: Microscopium is a minor constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere, one of twelve created in the 18th century by French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille and one of several depicting scientific instruments.

cards.name: Monoceros
cards.summary: Monoceros is a faint constellation on the celestial equator that represents a unicorn. Its definition is attributed to the 17th-century cartographer Petrus Plancius, though it may have appeared on a Persian sphere or in earlier works as the other Horse south of the Twins and the Crab.
cards.howToFind: Monoceros lies in a large but comparatively vacant field between the two Dogs, Orion, and the Hydra. It is best seen in February when it comes to the meridian due south from Procyon. The celestial equator passes through the figure lengthwise from the Belt of Orion to the tail of the animal, which sits just below the head of Hydra.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth for this constellation as it is a modern creation. While Petrus Plancius is credited with its definition, the astronomer Bartschius is generally supposed to have been first to chart it as Unicornu. It has also been associated with the alternative title Cervus and several Chinese asterisms including the Four Great Canals and the Outer Kitchen.

quotes.text: Monoceros, the Unicorn, das Einhorn in Germany, la Licorne in France, and il Unicorno or Licorno in Italy, lies in the large but comparatively vacant field between the two Dogs, Orion, and the Hydra
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Monoceros

cards.name: Musca
cards.summary: Musca is a small constellation in the deep southern sky representing a fly. It was one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the late sixteenth century.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Musca south of the Cross and east of the Chamaeleon, with parts of the figure lying in the Milky Way. It is highest in the evening sky around May and is fully visible to those located between latitudes fifteen degrees north and ninety degrees south.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this constellation as it was introduced at the end of the sixteenth century. It was originally known as Apis, the Bee, for two hundred years and was also called Musca Apis by Halley in 1679. Julius Schiller later attempted to unite it with the Bird of Paradise and the Chamaeleon to represent the biblical figure mother Eve.

quotes.text: This title generally is supposed to have been substituted by La Caille, about 1752, for Bayer's Apis, the Bee; but Halley, in 1679, had called it Musca Apis; and even previous to him, Riccioli catalogued it as Apis seu Musca.

cards.name: Norma
cards.summary: Norma is a small constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere that represents a right angle. It was one of twelve constellations drawn up in the 18th century by French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille to depict scientific instruments.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Norma between the constellations Ara and Lupus, just north of the Southern Triangle. It is highest in the sky around July and is fully visible for those located between latitudes 30 degrees north and 90 degrees south. The figure contains the star Yaqana and lies within the branches of the Milky Way.
cards.mythology: There is no traditional mythology associated with this figure as it was introduced in the 18th century. Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille created it to represent a rule, a carpenter's square, a set square or a level. It was originally composed of unformed stars from Ara and Lupus and was at one time associated with the constellation Circinus.

quotes.text: Norma is a small constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere between Ara and Lupus, one of twelve drawn up in the 18th century by French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille and one of several depicting scientific instruments.

quotes.text: Norma et Regula, the Level and Square, originally was composed of some unformed stars of Ara and Lupus, within the branches of the Milky Way, just north of Apus; but later it became the Southern Triangle of Theodor and Bayer.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Norma et Regula

cards.name: Octans
cards.summary: Octans is a faint constellation in the deep Southern Sky that represents the octant, a navigational instrument. It was devised by the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille in 1752 and is notable because the southern celestial pole is located within its boundaries.
cards.howToFind: Visible only from latitudes south of the equator, Octans is highest in the evening sky around September. Observers can locate the general area by following a straight line from Alpha Crucis to Beta Hydri, as the pole lies about one third of the distance from the latter star. It is surrounded by several constellations including Hydrus, Tucana, and Pavo, though it is often described as a blankness in the heavens due to its lack of bright stars.
cards.mythology: There is no myth associated with this constellation as it was introduced by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century. It was published in recognition of the octant invented in 1730 by John Hadley. While ancient writers like Ovid and Vergil made infrequent references to a south pole, early navigators often commented on the lack of identifiable stars in this specific region.

quotes.text: Octans Hadleianus, now known simply as Octans, was formed and published by La Caille in 1752 in recognition of the octant invented in 1730 by John Hadley.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Octans

quotes.text: The early navigators commented more or less correctly on the blankness of the heavens in this region, and Peter Martyr wrote : They knewe no starre there lyke unto this pole, that myght be decerned aboute the poynte;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Octans

cards.name: Ophiuchus
cards.summary: Ophiuchus is a large constellation straddling the celestial equator that represents a man grasping a snake. Its name is derived from the Ancient Greek word for serpent-bearer, and it was one of the forty-eight constellations originally listed by Ptolemy.
cards.howToFind: Look for this figure in the July sky between the latitudes of sixty degrees and minus seventy-six degrees. It is situated just east of the head of Hercules and north of Scorpius, where the figure appears to be standing on the scorpion with both feet. The constellation is marked by the bright stars Rasalhague at the head, Sabik at the knee, and the two stars Yed Prior and Yed Posterior forming one of the hands.
cards.mythology: This figure is generally identified as the great physician Aesculapius, who was educated by Apollo or the centaur Chiron. He became so skilled that he could restore the dead to life, including Hippolytus, whose members he glued back together. Fearing for the permanence of his kingdom, Pluto induced Jove to strike the physician with a thunderbolt and place him among the stars. The serpent he holds is a symbol of wisdom, renovation, and the power to discover healing herbs.

quotes.text: Both firmly clutch the Serpent, which encircles the waist of Ophiuchus, but he, stedfast with both his feet well set, tramples a huge monster, even the Scorpion, standing upright on his eye and breast.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Aesculapius was the earliest of his profession and the ship's surgeon of the Argo. When the famous voyage was over he became so skilled in practice that he even restored the dead to life, among these being Hippolytus
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Ophiuchus

quotes.text: The hoofs of the Horse, the head and neck of the Bird and Ophiuchus’ bright shoulders wheel along this circle in their course.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Orion
cards.summary: Orion is a prominent constellation that represents a giant hunter and warrior. It was among the forty-eight figures listed by Ptolemy in the second century and is recognized as one of the most brilliant stellar groups in the sky.
cards.howToFind: Orion is visible from every part of the globe and is highest during the evening in January. It is easily identified by the three stars of the glittering belt, Alnilam, Alnitak, and Mintaka, which lie aslant beneath the knees of the Bull. The hunter is further marked by the bright stars Rigel at the left foot and Betelgeuse at the right shoulder, with the constellation bordered by Taurus, Gemini, Monoceros, Lepus, and Eridanus.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, Orion was the tallest and most beautiful of men, a mighty hunter who served King Oenopion by smiting beasts with his club. He was eventually slain by a scorpion's sting, an event memorialized in the sky where he appears to flee at the western verge when the Scorpion rises in the east. Other traditions identify the figure as the giant Nimrod bound to the sky, or the Egyptian soul of Osiris.

quotes.text: Aslant beneath the fore-body of the Bull is set the great Orion. Let none who pass him spread out on high on a cloudless night imagine that, gazing on the heavens, one shall see other stars more fair.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: When the Scorpion comes Orion flies to utmost end of earth.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Orion

quotes.text: There is a tale told by the men of old, who said that stout Orion laid hands upon her robe, what time in Chios he was smiting with his strong club all manner of beasts, as a service of the hunt to that King Oenopion.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Pavo
cards.summary: Pavo is a constellation in the southern sky whose name is Latin for peacock. It was likely conceived by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman, first appearing on a celestial globe in 1598. Along with Grus, Phoenix, and Tucana, it is one of the four constellations collectively known as the Southern Birds.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find this figure in the southern sky between the latitudes of fifteen and negative ninety degrees. It is highest in the evening around August and is bordered by Indus, Apus, Ara, Octans, and Telescopium. The constellation contains the star named Peacock, which serves as a primary marker for the figure.
cards.mythology: The peacock was considered sacred to Juno, the immortal queen of the heavens, because its starry tail served as a symbol of immortality. According to one tradition, the constellation represents Argos, the builder of the ship Argo, who was changed by Juno into this bird when his vessel was transferred to the sky. In the seventeenth century, Julius Schiller attempted to unite these stars with Indus to form the biblical figure of Saint Job.

quotes.text: Pavo first appeared on a 35-cm (14 in) diameter celestial globe published in 1598 in Amsterdam by Petrus Plancius and Jodocus Hondius and was depicted in Johann Bayer's star atlas Uranometria of 1603
quotes.source: Wikipedia: Pavo (constellation)

quotes.text: This bird was still further astronomical in originally having been Argos, the builder of the ship Argo, who was changed by Juno to a peacock when his vessel was transferred to the sky, where he has since rejoined her.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Pavo

quotes.text: The title is an appropriate one for enduring stars, as this bird has long been a symbol of immortality, fancifully said to be from the annual renewing of its feathers;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Pavo

cards.name: Pegasus
cards.summary: Pegasus is a large constellation in the northern sky representing a winged horse. It was one of the original 48 figures listed by Ptolemy and is often depicted as a half-figure, as if partly hidden in the clouds.
cards.howToFind: The constellation is best seen in October and is easily identified by the Great Square, which is formed by the stars Algenib, Markab, Scheat, and Alpheratz. To a naked-eye observer, it lies north of Aquarius and Pisces and is bordered by Andromeda and Cygnus. The star Enif marks the nose of the horse, while the stars of the Great Square are said to be inclosing the body of the Horse.
cards.mythology: In Greek mythology, Pegasus was the son of Neptune and Medusa, born from the blood of his mother after Perseus severed her head. He was a favorite of the Muses because his hoof struck the earth on Mount Helicon and caused the fountain of Hippocrene to flow. The hero Bellerophon later rode him to slay the Chimaera, but when he attempted to fly to heaven, Jupiter caused an insect to sting the horse. Pegasus threw his rider and rose alone to become the Thundering Horse of Jove that carried the divine lightning.

quotes.text: He it was, men say, that brought down from lofty Helicon the bright water of bounteous Hippocrene. For not yet on Helicon’s summit trickled the fountain’s springs, but the Horse smote it and straightway the gushing water was shed abroad
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: That poetic steed, With beamy mane, whose hoof struck out from earth The fount of Hippocrene.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Pegasus

quotes.text: Parted at the navel, with only half a body, wheels in heaven the sacred Horse.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Perseus
cards.summary: Perseus is an ancient northern constellation representing the Greek hero who rescued Andromeda. It was one of the original forty-eight figures listed by Ptolemy and is located near other constellations from the same legend, including Cassiopeia and Andromeda.
cards.howToFind: Look for a tall figure in the Milky Way between Cassiopeia and Taurus, reaching its highest point in the evening around December. The constellation is marked by the bright stars Mirfak and Algol, and its right side forms a slight curve known as the Segment of Perseus. It is fully visible for observers between latitudes ninety degrees north and thirty-two degrees south.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, Perseus was the son of Danae who was sent to fetch the head of the mortal Gorgon, Medusa. Aided by Mercury, he used the shield of Minerva as a mirror to avoid being petrified by the Gorgon's gaze before lopping off her head. He later used this trophy to rescue Andromeda from a sea monster. Later interpretations sometimes identified the figure as David holding the head of Goliath or the Apostle Paul.

quotes.text: Her Perseus joyns, her Foot his Shoulder bears Proud of the weight, and mixes with her Stars.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Perseus

quotes.text: His right hand is stretched toward the throne of the mother of his bride, and, as if pursuing that which lies before his feet, he greatly strides, dust-stained, in the heaven of Zeus.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: In the mirror of his polished shield Reflected, saw Medusa slumbers take, And not one serpent by good chance awake; Then backward an unerring blow he sped, And from her body lopped at once her head.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Perseus

cards.name: Phoenix
cards.summary: Phoenix is a minor constellation in the southern sky named after the mythical bird of fire. It was first depicted on a celestial atlas by Johann Bayer in 1603 and is one of the four constellations known as the Southern Birds.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Phoenix between Eridanus and Grus, south of Fornax and Sculptor. It is fully visible between latitudes 32 and -90 degrees and is highest in the sky around November. The figure is marked by the stars Ankaa and Wurren, with Ankaa being quite conspicuous from its solitary position southeast from Fomalhaut.
cards.mythology: There is no classical Greek myth for this constellation as it was a new figure introduced by Bayer, though it was in a measure by adoption rather than by invention. The figure was previously known to Arabian astronomers as a primitive Boat or Young Ostriches, and others changed the figure to that of a Griffin or Eagle. In Egypt, the bird was known as Bennu and served as an emblem of immortality.

quotes.text: Phoenix, the French Phénix, the German Phönix, and the Italian Fenice, is one of Bayer's new figures, between Eridanus and Grus, south of Fornax and Sculptor, — its α, κ, μ, β, ν, and γ in a line curving toward the south like that of a primitive Boat, by which figure, as Al Zauraḳ, the Arabs knew them.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Phoenix

quotes.text: But, whether Bayer knew it or not, his title is an appropriate one, for with various early nations — at all events, in China, Egypt, India, and Persia — this bird has been "an astronomical symbol of cyclic period,"
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Phoenix

cards.name: Pictor
cards.summary: Pictor is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere that represents a painter's easel. It was introduced in the 18th century by Abbé Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille, who originally named it Equuleus Pictoris.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find this constellation in the southern sky between the bright star Canopus and the Large Magellanic Cloud. It is located south of Columba and is bordered by Caelum, Carina, Dorado, Puppis, and Volans. The figure is best seen around January and is fully visible to anyone located between latitudes 26 degrees north and 90 degrees south.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient mythology associated with this constellation as it was invented in the 18th century. It was formed and named by La Caille to represent the Painter's Easel.

quotes.text: Equuleus Pictoris, the Painter's Easel, was formed, and thus named, by La Caille, but also has been called Pluteum Pictoris; astronomers know it as Pictor.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Equuleus Pictoris

quotes.text: Normally represented as an easel, Pictor was named by Abbé Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century.

cards.name: Pisces
cards.summary: Pisces represents a pair of fishes connected by a cord and is a vast constellation of the zodiac. Its name is Latin for fishes and it marks the point where the ecliptic and the celestial equator intersect at the March equinox. The constellation is often referred to as the Leaders of the Celestial Host because it contains the equinoctial point known as the First of Aries.
cards.howToFind: Pisces is located between the smaller Aries to the east and Aquarius to the southwest. To find the northern fish, use the left shoulder of Andromeda as a guide, while the southwestern fish is positioned east of Pegasus. The figure is defined by stars such as Alrescha, which marks the knot in the connecting cords, and Yunyu, located above the ventral fin of the western fish. It is highest in the evening sky around November and is fully visible between latitudes 83 degrees North and 57 degrees South.
cards.mythology: Greek mythology identifies the figures as Aphrodite and her son Eros, who jumped into the Euphrates river to escape the monster Typhon and were transformed into fishes. Latin authors similarly described the fishes as the creatures that carried Venus and her boy out of danger, leading Manilius to write that Venus owed her safety to their shape. An older Syrian tradition associates the constellation with the goddess Derketo, who was depicted with a woman's head and a fish's body. In later Christian interpretations, the two fishes were sometimes said to represent the fish used by Christ to feed the five thousand.

quotes.text: Still father in front of the Ram and still in the vestibule of the South are the Fishes. Ever one is higher than the other, and louder hears the fresh rush of the North wind.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: The figures are widely separated in the sky, the northeastern one lying just south of β Andromedae, headed towards it, and the southwestern one east from and headed towards Aquarius and Pegasus, the lucida marking the knot of the connecting bands.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Pisces

quotes.text: And here fantastic fishes duskly float, Using the calm for waters, while their fires Throb out quick rhythms along the shallow air.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Pisces

cards.name: Piscis Austrinus
cards.summary: Piscis Austrinus is a constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere known as the southern fish. It was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy and is often depicted drinking the water flowing from the urn of Aquarius.
cards.howToFind: Look for this constellation in the southern sky where it is highest at 9pm around October. It is located south of Capricornus and Aquarius and contains the prominent star Fomalhaut, which marks the fish's mouth. Observers between latitudes 53 and -90 can see the full figure, including the stars Tiangang and Baijiu.
cards.mythology: In early legend, this figure was considered the parent of the two zodiacal fishes. While it is an ancient Greek constellation, some traditions associated it with the Syrian god Dagon or the Egyptian Phagre and Oxyrinque. Later Mosaicists interpreted the stars as the barrel of meal belonging to the widow of Sarephtha or the fish caught by St. Peter.

quotes.text: Below Aegoceros before the blasts of the South Wind swims a Fish, facing Cetus, alone and part from the former Fishes; and him men call the Southern Fish.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: In early legend our australis was the parent of the zodiacal two, and has always been known under this specific title, varied by the other adjectives of equivalent signification, austrinus, meridionalis, and notius.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Piscis Australis

quotes.text: One large and bright by both the Pourer's feet,

cards.name: Puppis
cards.summary: Puppis represents the stern of the ship Argo and is the largest of the three constellations formed from the division of the ancient Argo Navis. It is one of the eighty-eight modern constellations and was originally described as the rear section of the vessel used by the Argonauts.
cards.howToFind: Puppis is visible to observers south of 39 degrees north latitude and is highest in the evening sky around February. It is located east of Canis Major and south of Monoceros and Hydra, featuring the named stars Naos, Tureis, and Pipit. The constellation is described as being hauled stern-foremost beside the tail of the Great Dog.
cards.mythology: Puppis was part of the great ship Argo, which mythology says was built by Argos or Glaucus for Jason and the fifty Argonauts. Aided by Pallas Athene, the crew sailed from Thessaly to Colchis in search of the golden fleece before Athene placed the boat in the sky. Another tradition claims the figure represents the first ship to sail the ocean, which carried Danaos and his fifty daughters from Egypt to Rhodes.

quotes.text: Part moves dim and starless from the prow Up to the mast, but all the rest is bright;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Argo Navis

quotes.text: Beside the tail of the Great Dog the ship Argo is hauled stern-foremost. For not hers is the proper course of a ship in motion, but she is borne backwards, reversed even as real ships, when already the sailors turn the stern to the land as they enter the haven, and every one back-paddles the ship, but she rushing sternward lays hold of the shore.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Pyxis
cards.summary: Pyxis is a small and faint constellation in the southern sky representing a mariner's compass. It was introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century and is counted among the 88 modern constellations.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Pyxis in the southern sky during March when it is highest at nine in the evening. It is located near the constellations of Antlia, Hydra, Puppis, and Vela. The constellation is fully visible to anyone located between latitudes fifty-three degrees north and ninety degrees south.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient myth associated with this figure as it was formed by La Caille in the 18th century. He created it from stars in the Mast of Argo and associated it with the Ship, though this has been described as an anachronism. While some later astronomers attempted to reannex the stars to Argo, Gould eventually reinserted the constellation into the astronomical record in 1879.

quotes.text: Pyxis was formed by La Caille from stars in the Mast of Argo, and so associated with the Ship, although there, of course, it is an anachronism.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Pyxis

quotes.text: Abbreviated from Pyxis Nautica, its name is Latin for a mariner's compass.

cards.name: Reticulum
cards.summary: Reticulum is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky representing a small net or reticle. The name refers to a net of crosshairs at the focus of a telescope eyepiece that is used to measure star positions.
cards.howToFind: Observers can look for the figure between October and December, as it reaches its highest point around January. It is located north of Hydrus and neighbours Dorado and Horologium. The constellation is identified by the star Rhombus and is fully visible between latitudes -90 and 22.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient mythology for this constellation. It was first drawn by Isaak Habrecht as the Rhombus and was later adopted by La Caille as a memorial of the reticle which he used in making his celebrated southern observations.

quotes.text: Reticulum Rhomboidalis, the Rhomboidal Net, is generally supposed to be of La Caille's formation as a memorial of the reticle which he used in making his celebrated southern observations; but it was first drawn by Isaak Habrecht, of Strassburg, as the Rhombus

cards.name: Sagitta
cards.summary: Sagitta is a dim but distinctive constellation in the northern sky that represents an arrow. Although it is the third-smallest constellation and dates to antiquity, it was included among the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy.
cards.howToFind: Sagitta lies in the Milky Way directly north of Aquila and south of Vulpecula. An observer can identify its shape using the stars Shakh, Sham, Telum, and Zuoqi, which form a pattern described as the Well-shaped Dart. It is highest in the evening sky around August and is fully visible for observers between latitudes 90 degrees North and 69 degrees South.
cards.mythology: Eratosthenes claimed this was the arrow Apollo used to exterminate the Cyclopes, though others saw it as the weapon Hercules shot toward the Stymphalian birds. It has also been regarded as the arrow of Cupid or the weapon that slew the eagle of Jove. Because the figure is cast without a bow, some traditions suggest it is a stray weapon belonging to the nearby archer, Sagittarius.

quotes.text: There is in front another Arrow cast Without a bow; and by it flies the Bird Nearer the north.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Sagitta

quotes.text: Further up there is another Arrow shot – alone without a bow. By it is the Bird outspread nearer the North, but hard at hand another bird tosses in storm

cards.name: Sagittarius
cards.summary: Sagittarius is a zodiacal constellation in the Southern celestial hemisphere representing an archer. Commonly depicted as a centaur drawing a bow, it is one of the original forty-eight figures listed by the second-century astronomer Ptolemy.
cards.howToFind: Look for the Archer in the southern sky during August, when it reaches its highest point. It is located between Scorpius and Ophiuchus to the west and Capricornus to the east. The figure is distinguished by the stars Kaus Australis, Kaus Media, and Kaus Borealis forming the bow, with Nunki marking the arrow's vane and Alnasl at its point.
cards.mythology: Ancient Greeks understood this figure as a satyr or a centaur, though it is distinct from the larger southern Centaur. While some traditions associate it with Chiron, early classic descriptions by Eratosthenes identified it as a satyr. In another tradition, the earthly Chiron invented the constellation to guide the Argonauts on their expedition to Colchis.

quotes.text: For verily his great Bow does the Bowman draw close by the Scorpion’s sting, and a little in front stands the Scorpion at his rising, but the Archer rises right after him.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: glorious in his Cretian Bow, Centaur follows with an aiming Eye, His Bow full drawn and ready to let fly.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Sagittarius

quotes.text: his crown always appears near his fore feet, and his arrow is always aimed at the Scorpion's heart.

cards.name: Scorpius
cards.summary: Scorpius is an ancient zodiac constellation in the Southern celestial hemisphere that represents a scorpion. It is one of the oldest recognized figures in the sky, identified by Ptolemy and predating Greek culture.
cards.howToFind: Look for a distinct S-shaped figure near the center of the Milky Way during July. The constellation is marked by the fiery red star Antares at its heart and the stars Shaula and Lesath at the tip of its curved sting. It is situated between Libra to the west and Sagittarius to the east, with Ophiuchus standing directly above its body.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, this is the monster that slew the giant hunter Orion. According to one tale, Orion vexed Artemis, who roused up against him another kind of beast, even the Scorpion, who proving mightier wounded him and slew him. This is why Orion is said to flee below the western horizon whenever the Scorpion rises in the east. Classical authors also identified it as the creature that caused the runaway of the steeds of Apollo when Phaethon attempted to drive them.

quotes.text: The winding River will straightway sink in fair flowing ocean at the coming of Scorpion, whose rising puts to flight even the mighty Orion.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Classical authors saw in it the monster that caused the disastrous runaway of the steeds of Phoebus Apollo when in the inexperienced hands of Phaethon.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Scorpio

quotes.text: Whiles Scorpio, dreading Sagittarius' dart Whose bow prest bent in flight the string had slipped, Down slid into the ocean flood apart.

cards.name: Sculptor
cards.summary: Sculptor is a faint constellation in the southern sky that represents a sculptor. It was introduced by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century. Originally named Apparatus Sculptoris, the name was later shortened to its current form.
cards.howToFind: Sculptor is an inconspicuous figure located between Cetus and Phoenix. Observers can find it in the southern sky during November, when it is highest at nine in the evening. It is bordered by several constellations including Aquarius, Fornax, Grus, and Piscis Austrinus.
cards.mythology: There is no mythology associated with this constellation. It was formed by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century from stars between Cetus and Phoenix. He originally called it "l'Atelier du Sculpteur, the Sculptor's Studio or Workshop" to represent the tools of the trade.

quotes.text: Sculptor, as it is now generally known, was formed by La Caille from stars between Cetus and Phoenix. He called it l'Atelier du Sculpteur, the Sculptor's Studio or Workshop, which Burritt and others have changed to Officina Sculptoria, or occasionally Apparatus Sculptoris.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Sculptor

cards.name: Scutum
cards.summary: Scutum is a small constellation located just south of the celestial equator that represents a shield. It was originally named Scutum Sobiescianum by Johannes Hevelius in 1684 and is one of the 88 IAU designated constellations.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find this figure between the tail of the Serpent and the head of Sagittarius, just west of the feet of Antinoüs. The constellation is highest in the sky around August and is visible to anyone between 74 degrees north and 90 degrees south latitude. Its four brightest stars, including Tianbian, form a narrow diamond shape.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient mythology for this constellation as it was introduced by Johannes Hevelius in the 17th century. It was created as a tribute to the third John Sobieski, king of Poland, to honor his successful resistance of the Turks at Vienna in 1683. The figure is pictured as the king's coat of arms, featuring a cross on the shield and four stars on the border representing his four sons.

quotes.text: It is pictured as the Coat of Arms of the third John Sobieski, king of Poland, who so distinguished himself in the defensive wars of his native land, as well as in his successful resistance of the Turks in their march on Vienna
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Scutum Sobiescianum

quotes.text: Seven years subsequently this new constellation was named for him by Hewel, with a glowing tribute to his merit and heroic deeds; the sign of the Cross for which he fought being emblazoned on his Shield as we have it to‑day.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Scutum Sobiescianum

cards.name: Serpens
cards.summary: Serpens is a northern constellation that represents a starlit serpent and was one of the forty-eight figures listed by Ptolemy. It is unique among modern constellations because it is split into two non-contiguous parts known as Serpens Caput and Serpens Cauda. The figure is represented as passing behind the constellation Ophiuchus, which separates the head from the tail.
cards.howToFind: Serpens is best seen in July and is visible between latitudes 74 and -64 degrees. The head is located ten degrees south of Corona Borealis and twenty degrees due east of Arcturus, marked by a noticeable group of stars including Zhou and the brightest star Unukalhai. The figure then winds south toward Libra before turning northeast along the Milky Way to terminate at the star Alya, which lies south of the tail of Aquila.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, this figure is the serpent grasped by the hands of Ophiuchus. It has been associated with various figures including Aesculapius, Glaucus, and Laocoon, or identified as the Lernaean Hydra slain by Hercules. Before Greek influence, Arabian astronomy saw a different figure here called the Pasture, where certain stars in Serpens and Ophiuchus formed the northern and southern boundaries for a field of sheep.

quotes.text: Both firmly clutch the Serpent, which encircles the waist of Ophiuchus, but he, stedfast with both his feet well set, tramples a huge monster, even the Scorpion, standing upright on his eye and breast.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: The starry Serpent . . . Southward winding from the Northern Wain, Shoots to remoter spheres its glittering train.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Serpens

quotes.text: Toward the Crown leans the Serpent’s jaw, but beneath his coiling form seek thou for the mighty Claws; they are scant of light and nowise brilliant.

cards.name: Sextans
cards.summary: Sextans is a faint, minor constellation on the celestial equator representing the astronomical sextant. It was introduced in 1687 by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius to honor an instrument he used frequently in his observations.
cards.howToFind: This constellation is located between Leo and Hydra, sitting west of Crater. It is highest in the sky around April and is fully visible to observers between latitudes 79 degrees North and 83 degrees South. One can look for the frame of the instrument about nine degrees south by east from the star Regulus.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient myth for this constellation as it was introduced by Johannes Hevelius in the 17th century. Hevelius placed the instrument between Leo and Hydra because those animals were of a fiery nature according to astrologers. This served as a commemoration of the destruction of his house and instruments by fire in 1679, an event he described as when Vulcan overcame Urania.

quotes.text: Sextans Uraniae was formed by Hevelius to commemorate the Sextant so successfully used by him in stellar measurements at Dantzig from 1658 to 1679. The original figure comprised the twelve unclaimed stars between Leo Hydra, west of Crater;
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Sextans

quotes.text: Sextans is a faint, minor constellation on the celestial equator which was introduced in 1687 by Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius. Its name is Latin for the astronomical sextant, an instrument that Hevelius made frequent use of in his observations.

cards.name: Taurus
cards.summary: Taurus is one of the oldest constellations of the zodiac, dating back to the Early Bronze Age when it marked the spring equinox. Located in the northern celestial hemisphere, it is a large and prominent figure in the winter sky representing a bull. Its traditional symbol resembles a bull's head and its importance to the agricultural calendar influenced various bull figures in the mythologies of Ancient Sumer, Egypt, and Rome.
cards.howToFind: Look for the bull crouching aslant above Orion and between the constellations of Aries and Gemini. The figure is easily identified by the V-shaped group called the Hyades, which forms the bull's forehead and features the bright, ruddy star Aldebaran as the eye. The Pleiades cluster marks the bull's shoulder, while the stars Elnath and Tianguan represent the tips of its long horns. Taurus is highest in the evening sky around January and is fully visible to observers between latitudes -59 and 88.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, the constellation is often identified as the snowy white bull that swam away with Europa, which explains why only his forward parts are drawn while his flanks remain immersed in the waves. Another version suggests the figure is Io, a lover of Jupiter whom Juno changed into a cow. The two famous clusters within the constellation, the Hyades and Pleiades, are said to be the daughters of Atlas. The Hyades were the nurses of the infant Bacchus, while the Pleiades were turned into stars after grieving for their father or to escape the hunter Orion.

quotes.text: At the feet of Charioteer seek for the crouching horned Bull. Very lifelike are his signs; so clear defined his head: not by other sign would one mark the head of an ox, since in such wise those very stars, wheeling on either side, fashion it.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: The sign Taurus may have been the Cretan Bull; and a transit through that sign may have been the celestial Βόσπορος of the Argonautic voyage.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Taurus

quotes.text: Small and dim are they all alike, but widely famed they wheel in heaven at morn and eventide, by the will of Zeus, who bade them tell of the beginning of Summer and Winter and of the coming of the ploughing-time.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Telescopium
cards.summary: Telescopium is a minor constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere representing a scientific instrument. It was one of twelve constellations named in the 18th century by French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
cards.howToFind: Look for this constellation in the southern sky between Ara and Sagittarius on the edge of the Milky Way. It is best seen in August, culminating at the same time as Wega of the Lyre, and is fully visible to observers south of 33 degrees north latitude. The figure is bordered by Pavo, Indus, and Corona Australis.
cards.mythology: There is no traditional mythology associated with this constellation as it was introduced in the 18th century. Lacaille created it to represent the telescope, and its name is a Latinized form of the Greek word for telescope. While it lacks Western lore, Chinese astronomy identified the star alpha as We, Danger, and gamma as the mythological Chuen Shwo.

quotes.text: Telescopium was later much reduced in size by Francis Baily and Benjamin Gould.
quotes.source: Wikipedia: Telescopium

quotes.text: Telescopium, or Tubus Astronomicus, was formed by La Caille between Ara and Sagittarius on the edge of the Milky Way, but in such irregular form that it encroached upon four of the old constellations;

cards.name: Triangulum
cards.summary: Triangulum is a small, ancient constellation in the northern sky whose name is Latin for triangle. It was known to the Greeks and Babylonians and was included in the 2nd century catalogue of Ptolemy.
cards.howToFind: Look for a long and narrow scalene triangle located south from Gamma Andromedae on the edge of the Milky Way. The figure is formed by the stars Alaybasan, Mothallah, and Apdu, situated between Andromeda, Aries, Perseus, and Pisces. It is highest in the evening sky during December and is visible from most latitudes except the far south.
cards.mythology: The Greeks called it Deltoton because it resembled their letter Delta. It was later associated with the island of Sicily, which Ceres is said to have begged Jove to reproduce in the heavens. Other traditions linked its shape to the Nile Delta, calling it the Gift of the Nile, or to the three parts of the earth: Europe, Asia, and Africa.

quotes.text: Below Andromeda, in three sides measured Like-to‑a‑Delta; equal two of them As it has, less the third, yet good to find The sign, than many better stored with stars.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Triangulum

quotes.text: There is also another sign, fashioned near, below Andromeda, Deltoton, drawn with three sides, whereof two appear equal but the third is less, yet very easy to find, for beyond many is it endowed with stars.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Triangulum Australe
cards.summary: Triangulum Australe is a small constellation in the far Southern Celestial Hemisphere whose name is Latin for "the southern triangle". It was first depicted on a celestial globe by Petrus Plancius in 1589 and later appeared with more accuracy in Johann Bayer's 1603 Uranometria.
cards.howToFind: Observers can locate this constellation between the latitudes of twenty degrees north and ninety degrees south, where it appears highest in the sky around July. It is identified by the acute, almost equilateral pattern of its three brightest stars, including the star named Atria. It lies south of Ara and is bordered by the constellations Apus, Circinus, and Norma.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this figure as it was introduced in the late sixteenth century. The scholar Caesius called it the Three Patriarchs, doubtless Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, from its three prominent stars. Julius Schiller also used the alphabetical title Signum Tau for the constellation.

quotes.text: Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle much more noticeable than its northern original, first appeared in print in Bayer's Uranometria of 1603, although its formation is attributed to Pieter Theodor of nearly a century previous.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Triangulum Australe

quotes.text: Its name is Latin for "the southern triangle", which distinguishes it from Triangulum in the northern sky and is derived from the acute, almost equilateral pattern of its three brightest stars.

cards.name: Tucana
cards.summary: Tucana is a constellation in the southern sky named after the toucan, a South American bird. It is one of twelve constellations conceived in the late sixteenth century by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman. Along with Grus, Phoenix, and Pavo, it is collectively known as the Southern Birds.
cards.howToFind: Tucana is fully visible to observers between latitudes 14 and -90 degrees and is highest in the evening sky around October. It lies immediately south of Phoenix and borders other constellations such as Grus, Indus, and the south polar Octans. Observers can look for the star Lang-Exster or the celebrated ball of suns known as cluster 47, which shines like a hazy star.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this constellation as it was introduced in the late sixteenth century by Petrus Plancius. The Chinese later translated the name as Neaou Chuy, meaning the Beak Bird, which was considered very appropriate to a creature that is almost all beak. In the 17th century, it was known by various names including the Brasilian Pye and the American Gans.

quotes.text: Tucana lies immediately south of Phoenix, bordering on the south polar Octans, its tail close to the bright Achernar of Eridanus, and marks the crossing of the equinoctial colure and the antarctic circle.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Tucana

quotes.text: The Chinese translated the original word, given to them by the Jesuits, as Neaou Chuy, the Beak Bird, very appropriate to a creature that is almost all beak.

cards.name: Ursa Major
cards.summary: Ursa Major, known as the Great Bear, is the third largest of the 88 modern constellations and was one of the original 48 listed by Ptolemy. Its Latin name means greater bear, contrasting it with the nearby Ursa Minor.
cards.howToFind: Ursa Major is highest in the sky around April and is fully visible between latitudes -16 and 90. A naked-eye observer can identify the seven stars of the Big Dipper, including the Pointers Dubhe and Merak, which lead the eye toward the pole-star. The figure is surrounded by neighbours such as Draco, Boötes, and Leo.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, the nymph Kallisto was changed into a bear by Juno's jealousy and later fixed in the northern skies by Jove. An older tradition from Crete identifies the constellation as one of the nurses who nurtured the infant Zeus in a cave on Mount Ida. Other cultures have viewed these stars as a Great Wagon, a Plough, or even a Bier followed by daughters acting as mourners.

quotes.text: The legend of Kallisto, the beloved of Zeus and mother of Arkas, has nothing to do with the original meaning of the stars. On the contrary, Kallisto was supposed to have been changed into the Arktos or Greater Bear because she was the mother of Arkas, that is to say, of the Arcadian or bear race, and her name, or that of her son, reminded the Greeks of their long established name of the northern constellation.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Ursa Major

quotes.text: If, indeed, the tale be true, from Crete they by the will of mighty Zeus entered up into heaven, for that when in olden days he played as a child in fragrant Dicton, near the hill of Ida, they set him in a cave and nurtured him for the space of a year, what time the Dictaean Curetes were deceiving Cronus.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: There the revolving Bear, which the Wain they call, was ensculptured, Circling on high, and in all its course regarding Orion; Sole of the starry train which refuses to bathe in the Ocean;

cards.name: Ursa Minor
cards.summary: Ursa Minor, also known as the Little Bear, is a constellation located in the far northern sky. It was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy and has traditionally been important for navigation because of Polaris being the north pole star. The constellation was suggested to Greek mariners around 600 B.C. by Thales, who was inspired by its use in Phoenicia.
cards.howToFind: Ursa Minor is fully visible between latitudes 0 and 90 degrees and is highest in the evening sky around June. To find it, look for seven stars forming a pattern known as the Little Dipper, with four stars in its bowl and three in the handle. The constellation is enclosed on three sides by the coils of Draco and neighbors Cepheus and Camelopardalis. The brightest star, Polaris, marks the end of the tail, while the stars Kochab and Pherkad form the outer edge of the bowl.
cards.mythology: According to classical lore, the stars of the two Bears represent sister nymphs who served as nurses on Mount Ida for the infant Jove. A tale from Crete says they set him in a cave and nurtured him for a year to hide him from Cronus. Another legend identifies the figure as Cynosura, a name often translated as the dog's tail. Some accounts link the constellation to Arcas, the son of Kallisto, who was transferred to the skies by his father Jove.

quotes.text: The other, less in size but valued more by sailors, Circles with all her stars in smaller orbit.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Ursa Minor

quotes.text: It is by Helice that the Achaeans on the sea divine which way to steer their ships, but in the other the Phoenicians put their trust when they cross the sea.
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: Then, too, the head of Kynosure runs very high, When night begins.

cards.name: Vela
cards.summary: Vela is a southern constellation whose name is Latin for the sails of a ship. It was originally part of a much larger figure called Argo Navis, which represented the ship used by Jason and the Argonauts, before being divided into three smaller parts.
cards.howToFind: Vela is highest in the evening sky around March and is fully visible to observers south of 34 degrees north latitude. It is located between the constellations of Antlia, Puppis, and Carina, and contains the bright stars Alsephina, Suhail, and Markeb. Along with stars in Carina, the stars Delta and Kappa Velorum form a prominent asterism known as the False Cross.
cards.mythology: Vela represents the sails of the Argo, the ship built by Argos for Jason and his crew of fifty demi-gods. According to Greek tradition, Pallas Athene aided the construction and placed the vessel in the sky after the expedition to find the golden fleece was complete. Other traditions suggest the figure represents the first ship to sail the ocean, which carried Danaos and his daughters from Egypt to Greece.

quotes.text: Sternforward thus is Jason's Argō drawn.

cards.name: Virgo
cards.summary: Virgo is a zodiacal constellation representing a maiden and is the second-largest figure in the entire sky. The sun passes through this region during the September equinox, and the figure is traditionally depicted holding a palm branch and an ear of wheat.
cards.howToFind: Observers can locate this constellation in the southern sky by finding its brightest star, Spica, which marks the ear of corn in the maiden's hand. The figure is highest at nine in the evening during May and is situated between Leo to the west and Libra to the east. A right-angled triangle of stars including Porrima, Zaniah, and Minelauva helps outline the kennel corner near the maiden's wings.
cards.mythology: In Greek lore, she is often identified as Justice, the daughter of Astraeus, who lived among humans during the Golden Age. As humanity declined into the Silver and Bronze Ages, she rebuked their growing wickedness and eventually fled to the heavens. Other traditions associate her with Persephone, daughter of Demeter, or the goddess Isis, who was said to have dropped wheat ears to form the Milky Way.

quotes.text: Beneath both feet of Boötes mark the Maiden, who in her hands bears the gleaming Ear of Corn. Whether she be daughter of Astraeus, who, men say, was of old the father of the stars, or child of other sire, untroubled be her course!
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

quotes.text: The last gleanings of the last field are bound up in a rude imitation of the human shape, and dressed in some rag-tags of finery. The usage has fallen into the conservative hands of children, but of old "the Maiden" was a regular image of the harvest-goddess, which, with a sickle and sheaves in her arms, attended by a crowd of reapers, and accompanied with music, followed the last carts home to the farm.
quotes.source: Richard Hinckley Allen, Star-Names and Their Meanings (1899): Virgo

quotes.text: “Behold what manner of race the fathers of the Golden Age left behind them! Far meaner than themselves! But ye will breed a viler progeny! Verily wars and cruel bloodshed shall be unto men and grievous woe shall be laid upon them.”
quotes.source: Aratus, Phaenomena, translated by G. R. Mair (Loeb Classical Library, 1921)

cards.name: Volans
cards.summary: Volans is a constellation in the southern sky that represents a flying fish. Its name is a shortened form of its original name, Piscis Volans, and it was one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius in the late sixteenth century.
cards.howToFind: Observers can find Volans in the southern sky between latitudes 15 and -90 degrees, where it is highest at 9pm around March. It is located south of the stars Canopus and Miaplacidus and is bordered by the constellations Carina, Chamaeleon, Dorado, Mensa, and Pictor.
cards.mythology: There is no classical myth associated with this constellation as it was introduced by Petrus Plancius from observations by Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman. While it represents a flying fish, Julius Schiller once included it in his biblical figure of Abel the Just.

quotes.text: Volans was one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman and it first appeared on a 35-cm (14") diameter celestial globe published in 1597
quotes.source: Wikipedia: Volans

quotes.text: Piscis Volans, the Flying Fish, now known by astronomers as Volans, is the Poisson Volant of the French and the Fliegende Fisch of the Germans. The Rudolphine Tables have it Passer, the Sparrow, and, as such, it is translated Fe Yu by the Chinese.

cards.name: Vulpecula
cards.summary: Vulpecula is a faint constellation in the Northern Sky that represents a little fox. It was identified in the 17th century and is located in the middle of the Summer Triangle.
cards.howToFind: Look for the constellation between the Arrow and the Swan in the region where the Milky Way divides into two branches. It is highest in the sky around September and is visible to observers between latitudes 90 degrees North and 61 degrees South. Its brightest star is Anser, which is located just west of the Fox's head.
cards.mythology: There is no ancient mythology for this figure as it is a modern constellation. It was introduced by Hevelius, who placed a fox and a goose in this space because he considered the animal to be very cunning, voracious and fierce. He chose this placement because the nearby constellations of the Eagle and the Vultur Cadens were of a similarly rapacious and greedy nature.
